qs.q: A nursing student is reviewing normal movement and alignment before skills lab. Which statement about body alignment (posture) is correct?
c: It is optimal musculoskeletal balance and operation with no undue strain on the joints, muscles, tendons, or ligaments
It is the use of major, stronger muscle groups to produce purposeful movement
It is the maintenance of body position and equilibrium by inner ear sensory organs
It is the design of equipment and work tasks to fit the capability of the worker
qs.e: Body alignment (posture) means optimal musculoskeletal balance and operation with no undue strain on joints, muscles, tendons, or ligaments. The last option describes ergonomics, not posture.

qs.q: Balance exists when the center of gravity is close to its ______ of support and the object has a wide base of support.
qs.e: Balance depends on keeping the center of gravity close to the base of support and using a wide base of support.

qs.q: Which statements about balance are correct? Select all that apply.
c: Balance is improved when the center of gravity is close to the base of support
A wide base of support improves balance
Spreading the feet apart and flexing the hips and knees increases body balance
Balance is greatest when the feet are kept together and the knees are locked
Flexing the hips and knees increases musculoskeletal strain
A narrow base of support makes lifting safer
qs.e: Balance improves with the center of gravity near a wide base of support, and increases when the feet are spread and hips and knees are flexed—this decreases musculoskeletal strain. Keeping feet together, locking the knees, or using a narrow base does the opposite.

qs.q: The nurse is teaching a client how to pick up a heavy box from the floor. Which action best increases body balance and reduces strain?
c: Spread the feet apart and flex the hips and knees
Keep the feet together and the knees locked
Bend from the waist with the legs straight
Twist the trunk while lifting to place the box on the counter
qs.e: Spreading the feet and flexing the hips and knees widens the base of support and lowers the center of gravity, increasing balance and decreasing musculoskeletal strain. Bending from the waist or twisting uses the vulnerable back instead.

qs.q: Coordinated body movement means muscles working together for purposeful movement, using ______ muscle groups.
qs.e: Coordinated movement uses the major and stronger muscle groups rather than the weaker back muscles.

qs.q: Which statements describe postural reflexes? Select all that apply.
c: They maintain body position and equilibrium during rest or movement
They include sensory organs in the inner ear
They include vision
They include autonomic contractions
They are voluntary movements that require conscious thought
They replace the need for coordinated body movement
qs.e: Postural reflexes maintain position and equilibrium during rest or movement and involve inner ear sensory organs, vision, and autonomic contractions. They are reflexive, not voluntary thought-driven movements.

qs.q: A client maintains body position and equilibrium while turning in bed without thinking about it. Which concept does this represent?
c: Postural reflexes
Coordinated body movement
Body alignment
Ergonomics
qs.e: Postural reflexes maintain body position and equilibrium during rest or movement. Coordinated body movement refers to muscles working together for purposeful movement.

qs.q: Which are developmental considerations that affect movement and alignment? Select all that apply.
c: Infant
Toddler
Adolescent
Older adult
Blood type
Dominant hand
qs.e: Developmental considerations range from infant through toddler, child, adolescent, adult, and older adult. Blood type and dominant hand are not listed developmental factors affecting movement and alignment.

qs.q: A student asks what is meant by activities of daily living (ADLs). Which response is correct?
c: Self-care activities that maintain a person's quality of life, such as eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting
Reflexive movements that maintain equilibrium during rest or movement
Exercises designed to improve bone formation and muscle development
Work tasks designed to conform to the capability of the worker
qs.e: ADLs are self-care activities that maintain quality of life, such as eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting. The last option defines ergonomics.

qs.q: Name the fourth ADL listed: eating, bathing, dressing, and ______.
qs.e: The listed ADLs are eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting—self-care activities that maintain quality of life.

qs.q: Which are postural abnormalities (congenital or acquired) that affect movement and alignment? Select all that apply.
c: Hip dysplasia
Torticollis
Scoliosis
Osteoporosis
Muscular dystrophy
Arthritis
qs.e: Hip dysplasia, torticollis, and scoliosis are postural abnormalities. Osteoporosis and muscular dystrophy fall under bone formation/muscle development, and arthritis affects joint/bone mobility.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with muscular dystrophy. Under which category of physical health factors does this condition fall?
c: Bone formation and muscle development
Postural abnormalities (congenital or acquired)
Joint and bone mobility
Central nervous system
qs.e: Dwarfism, osteoporosis, and muscular dystrophy reflect bone formation and muscle development. Torticollis is a postural abnormality and arthritis is a joint/bone mobility problem.

qs.q: Which factors affect joint and bone mobility? Select all that apply.
c: Arthritis
Trauma
Smoking
Depression
Sedentary lifestyle
Diet
qs.e: Joint and bone mobility is affected by arthritis and trauma. Smoking, depression, sedentary lifestyle, and diet are mental health and lifestyle factors instead.

qs.q: A client who had a spinal cord injury now has impaired movement and alignment. This falls under which category of factors?
c: Postural abnormalities (congenital or acquired)
Bone formation or muscle development
Joint or bone mobility
Central nervous system
qs.e: Stroke and spinal cord injury are central nervous system factors affecting movement and alignment. Trauma is listed under joint and bone mobility, which is the tempting but incorrect choice here.

qs.q: A client with depression has been sitting in the same position all day. Which areas does depression affect?
c: Activity level, posture, and energy to perform ADLs
Only the client's ability to eat and swallow
Vision and inner ear sensory function
Bone density and adult height
qs.e: Depression affects activity level, posture, and energy to perform ADLs. Vision and inner ear function relate to postural reflexes, not depression.

qs.q: Which lifestyle factors affect movement and alignment? Select all that apply.
c: Diet
Sedentary versus active lifestyle
Smoking
Culture and values
Hip dysplasia
Torticollis
qs.e: Lifestyle factors include diet, sedentary versus active living, smoking, and culture and values. Hip dysplasia and torticollis are postural abnormalities under physical health.

qs.q: The nurse is planning an activity program for a client whose culture places little emphasis on exercise. Which statement is correct?
c: Cultures have differing emphasis on the importance of movement and exercise
Culture has no influence on a client's activity level
Culture affects only dietary preferences and not movement
Culture determines a client's center of gravity and base of support
qs.e: Cultures have differing emphasis on the importance of movement and exercise, which is a lifestyle factor affecting alignment and activity. Culture is not a biomechanical factor like center of gravity.

qs.q: Ergonomics designs equipment and work tasks to conform to the ______ of the worker.
qs.e: Ergonomics conforms equipment and tasks to the capability of the worker and adjusts the work environment and practices to prevent injuries.

qs.q: A nurse manager redesigns lifting tasks on the unit and adjusts the work environment to prevent staff injuries. This is an example of:
c: Ergonomics
Body alignment
Postural reflexes
Coordinated body movement
qs.e: Ergonomics is the practice of designing equipment and work tasks to conform to the capability of the worker and adjusting the work environment to prevent injuries. Body alignment is an individual's posture, not a work redesign.

qs.q: During which everyday activities should the nurse use proper body movement to build good habits? Select all that apply.
c: Moving a medication cart
Pushing a bed
Reaching to silence an alarm
Wearing gloves before giving an injection
Checking the medication record against the provider's order
Documenting after the procedure
qs.e: Even simple activities such as moving a medication cart, pushing a bed, and reaching to silence an alarm require proper body movement to develop good habits while engaging the musculoskeletal system. Infection control and documentation tasks are not listed movement activities.

qs.q: To obtain maximum power, the nurse uses the longest and strongest muscles of the ______ and ______.
qs.e: The longest and strongest muscles are in the arms and legs, which should do the work rather than the back.

qs.q: A new nurse lifts a client by bending from the waist. Which muscle group is at risk because it is weaker and prone to injury when used improperly?
c: Back muscles
Leg muscles
Arm muscles
Gluteal muscles
qs.e: Back muscles are weaker and prone to injury when used improperly; the longest and strongest muscles of the arms and legs should be used for maximum power so most of the burden is borne by the legs and arms rather than the back. Engaging the core (gluteal muscles contracted downward, abdominal muscles upward) stabilizes the pelvis and protects the abdomen.

qs.q: Which actions are correct when moving a client or object to prevent injury? Select all that apply.
c: Engage core muscles to stabilize the pelvis and protect the abdomen
Contract the gluteal muscles downward
Contract the abdominal muscles upward
Keep an erect posture with correct alignment
Hold the breath during the lift to increase abdominal pressure
Let the arms bear the entire load
qs.e: Engaging the core stabilizes the pelvis and protects the abdomen, with the gluteal muscles contracted downward and the abdominal muscles upward, while maintaining an erect posture with correct alignment. Holding the breath is not described, and most of the burden should be borne by the legs and arms rather than the back or arms alone.

qs.q: When engaging the core, the nurse contracts the gluteal muscles ______.
qs.e: The gluteal muscles are contracted downward while the abdominal muscles are contracted upward to stabilize the pelvis and protect the abdomen.

qs.q: The nurse works as close as possible to the client before turning the client in bed. What is the rationale?
c: The body's center of gravity stays close to the object, so most of the burden is borne by the legs and arms rather than the back
Standing close makes the back muscles stronger during the move
Standing close narrows the base of support for better stability
Standing close eliminates the need to engage the core muscles
qs.e: Working close to the object keeps the center of gravity near it so the legs and arms bear the burden instead of the back. A narrow base of support actually reduces balance, so that distractor is wrong.

qs.q: The nurse is pushing a client's bed down the hallway and turns the body sideways to look behind. Which action requires correction?
c: Twisting the body instead of facing the direction of movement
Facing the direction of movement
Pushing the bed with the whole body
Keeping the arms close to the body while pushing
qs.e: The nurse should face the direction of movement and never twist the body. Pushing with the whole body and keeping arms close are correct technique.

qs.q: Which pushing techniques prevent injury? Select all that apply.
c: Push rather than pull when possible
Keep the arms close to the body
Push with the whole body
Twist from the trunk to gain extra force
Pull the object toward you whenever possible
Keep the arms extended away from the body
qs.e: Push rather than pull, keep arms close, and push with the whole body. Pulling, twisting, and reaching with extended arms strain the back and are not recommended.

qs.q: To broaden the base of support, the nurse spreads the feet ______ apart and flexes the knees.
qs.e: Broadening the base of support means spreading the feet shoulder width apart and flexing the knees.

qs.q: The nurse prepares to move a client up in bed. Which body position best applies the ergonomics principles described?
c: Spread the feet shoulder width apart and flex the knees
Stand on the toes with the knees straight
Reach across the bed with one arm fully extended
Twist at the waist to gain leverage on the client
qs.e: Spreading the feet shoulder width apart and flexing the knees broadens the base of support and lowers strain. Reaching across the bed moves the center of gravity away from the body and twists the spine.

qs.q: When assessing the client before a move (step 1), which actions are included? Select all that apply.
c: Determine the client's ability to understand instruction and cooperate with the movement
Know the client's medical diagnosis, health issues, and movement capabilities
Apply braces or devices necessary for movement
Encourage the client to assist as much as permitted to promote independence
Begin the transfer first and assess afterward
Assume the client can fully participate without assessment
qs.e: Step 1 is assessing the client and the ability to assist, including cognition/cooperation, diagnosis and movement capabilities, braces or devices, and encouraging assistance within capability to promote independence. Skipping assessment risks injury to client and staff.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to transfer a client from bed to a chair. Which action is performed first?
c: Assess the client and the ability to assist with the planned movement
Elevate the bed to a comfortable working height
Lock the wheels of the bed
Decide which equipment to use
qs.e: The first step in ensuring safe patient handling is assessing the client and the ability to assist with the planned movement. Elevating the bed, locking wheels, and choosing equipment come later in the sequence.

qs.q: A client reports severe pain and must be moved to a gurney. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Administer the prescribed analgesic prior to movement
Hold the analgesic until after the transfer is complete
Give only nonpharmacologic measures and delay the prescribed medication
Move the client quickly to minimize the time in pain
qs.e: Step 7 is to administer the prescribed analgesic if the client is in pain prior to movement. Moving a client in pain before medication increases guarding, uncoordinated movement, and injury risk.

qs.q: The nurse ensures that enough ______ are available and present to safely move the patient (step 2).
qs.e: Step 2 is ensuring that enough staff are available and present to safely move the client.

qs.q: When assessing the area before a move (step 3), which actions are included? Select all that apply.
c: Assess for clutter
Assess accessibility to the patient
Assess availability of devices
Remove any obstacles or barriers
Move the client first and clear the area afterward
Leave equipment in the pathway so it is within reach
qs.e: Step 3 is assessing the area for clutter, accessibility to the client, and availability of devices, then removing obstacles or barriers. Obstacles left in the pathway create a fall and injury hazard.

qs.q: Before choosing a lift device for a client, the nurse uses a screening or assessment tool. This action represents which step?
c: Step 2
Step 4
Step 6
Step 9
qs.e: Using a screening or assessment tool is step 4; step 5 is deciding which equipment to use, and step 9 is locking the wheels.

qs.q: After using a screening or assessment tool (step 4), the nurse's next action is to decide which ______ to use (step 5).
qs.e: Step 5 is deciding which equipment to use, based on the client assessment and screening tool results.

qs.q: The nurse has assessed the client, prepared the area, and selected the equipment. Which action comes next?
c: Plan carefully and communicate to care team members and the patient
Lock the wheels of the bed
Move the patient in a smooth, rhythmic motion
Assess the patient's ability to assist with the movement
qs.e: Step 6 is planning carefully and communicating the plan to care team members and the client; the analgesic step (7) follows. Assessing the client was step 1 and is already done.

qs.q: Which actions ensure patient safety during the transfer (step 10)? Select all that apply.
c: Avoid friction on the skin
Support the body properly with good alignment
Avoid grabbing the client
Move in a smooth, rhythmic motion
Move in quick, jerky motions to save time
Grab the client under the arm to secure the hold
qs.e: During transfer, avoid skin friction, support the body properly with good alignment, avoid grabbing, and move in a smooth, rhythmic motion. Grabbing or jerky movement causes skin injury and uncoordinated lifts.

qs.q: During a transfer, the nurse moves the client in a smooth, ______ motion.
qs.e: A smooth, rhythmic motion prevents uncoordinated lifts and protects both the client and the nurse.

qs.q: The nurse is transferring a client from bed to a gurney. Which action prevents the bed from moving during the transfer?
c: Lock the wheels
Elevate only the head of the bed
Remove the side rails and leave the bed unlocked
Ask the client to hold the bed rail during the transfer
qs.e: Locking the wheels (step 9) keeps the bed stable during transfer. An unlocked bed can roll, causing an uncoordinated lift and a fall.

qs.q: Which practices lead to patient handling injuries? Select all that apply.
c: Uncoordinated lifts
High exertion while in an awkward position
Manual lifting and transferring without assistive devices
Using a gait belt during a transfer
Pushing rather than pulling
Locking the wheels before a transfer
qs.e: Uncoordinated lifts, high exertion in awkward positions, and manual lifting without assistive devices all cause handling injuries. Using devices, pushing rather than pulling, and locking wheels are protective behaviors.

qs.q: Which additional factors lead to patient handling injuries? Select all that apply.
c: Repetitive movements such as lifting, transferring, and repositioning patients
Lifting while fatigued
Standing for long periods
Using powered full-body lifts
Spreading the feet to broaden the base of support
Engaging the core muscles during a lift
qs.e: Repetitive movements, lifting while fatigued, and prolonged standing contribute to handling injuries. Powered lifts, a broad base of support, and core engagement reduce risk.

qs.q: Which client places the nurse at greatest risk for a patient handling injury?
c: A client with a cognitive impairment who is dependent and unable to actively participate in the move
A client who can stand and pivot with a gait belt
A client who repositions independently in bed
A client ambulating in the hallway with a walker
qs.e: Transferring or repositioning clients with cognitive impairments, who are dependent or obese, or who are unable or unwilling to participate creates the greatest handling risk. Clients who assist with movement reduce the load on the nurse.

qs.q: Repetitive movements such as lifting, transferring, and ______ patients contribute to handling injuries.
qs.e: Repositioning is listed along with lifting and transferring as a repetitive movement that leads to patient handling injuries.

qs.q: Which devices aid in mobility? Select all that apply.
c: Friction-reducing sheets
Gait belts
Standing assist device
Lateral assist device
An incentive spirometer
Oxygen saturation monitor
qs.e: Friction-reducing sheets, gait belts, standing assist, and lateral assist devices are listed mobility devices. Breathing and monitoring equipment do not aid mobility.

qs.q: A client cannot bear weight and requires a complete transfer from bed to chair. Which device is most appropriate?
c: Powered full-body lift
Gait belt
Friction-reducing sheet
Lateral assist device
qs.e: Powered full-body lifts are listed among the devices that aid in mobility for a full transfer. Gait belts and assist devices require the client to bear some weight or assist.

qs.q: Name the device used to aid in mobility that the nurse holds while ambulating a client: a ______.
qs.e: Gait belts are listed as devices to aid in mobility and are used for support during ambulation and transfers.

qs.q: Which skills lab activities are listed for patient positioning and movement? Select all that apply.
c: Turning the patient in bed
Moving a patient up in bed
Moving a patient from bed to a gurney
Moving a patient from bed to chair
Inserting a urinary catheter
Changing a sterile dressing
qs.e: Turning in bed, moving up in bed, bed to gurney, and bed to chair are listed skills lab activities. Catheter insertion and sterile dressing changes are not part of this list.

qs.q: Which skill is included in the listed skills lab activities for patient movement?
c: Dangling a patient
Inserting a urinary catheter
Performing a sterile wound dressing change
Administering an IV push medication
qs.e: Dangling a patient and ambulating a patient are both listed skills lab activities. The other options are not part of this movement and positioning skills list.

qs.q: Two transfer skills listed are moving a patient from bed to a gurney and moving a patient from bed to a ______.
qs.e: The listed transfers are bed to gurney and bed to chair, alongside turning, moving up in bed, ambulating, and dangling.

qs.q: Which statement best defines communication?
c: Speaking clearly enough that another person can repeat the words
Exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between two or more people
Sending information without needing a receiver
Using spoken language rather than body language
qs.e: Communication involves exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between people. It is broader than speaking clearly and includes nonverbal forms.

qs.q: Which outcomes or conditions are linked to communication in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Establishing a healthy work environment
Sustaining a healthy work environment
Providing safe care
Providing quality care
Guaranteeing that every message is successful
qs.e: The slides directly link communication to establishing and sustaining a healthy work environment and providing safety and quality care. They do not guarantee that communication is always successful.

qs.q: The communication participant who initiates information is the sender, also called the _____.
qs.e: The sender is the encoder and initiates information. The decoder is the receiver, not the initiator.

qs.q: The actual communication product from the source, which may be visual, auditory, or kinesthetic, is the _____.
qs.e: The message is the actual communication product. The channel describes how that information is sent.

qs.q: The audio, visual, or kinesthetic means by which information is sent is the _____.
qs.e: The channel is how information is sent. It is distinct from the message, which is the communication product itself.

qs.q: The person to whom a message is sent is the receiver, also called the _____.
qs.e: The receiver is the decoder. The encoder is the sender who initiates the information.

qs.q: The response a receiver sends back to the sender is called _____.
qs.e: Feedback is the receiver's response to the sender. It is not the channel used to transmit the original message.

qs.q: A nurse explains a procedure to a client using spoken words. Which characteristic identifies this as verbal communication?
c: It relies on language
It depends only on facial expression
It excludes the exchange of meaning
It is a form of silence
qs.e: The slides describe verbal communication as spoken and reliant on language. Facial expressions and silence are listed as nonverbal communication.

qs.q: Which observations represent nonverbal communication? Select all that apply.
c: Touch and eye contact
Facial expressions, posture, and gait
Gestures and physical appearance, including dress and grooming
Sounds and silence
Spoken words that rely on language
A written e-mail message
qs.e: The slides include all of these body-language cues, sounds, and silence as nonverbal communication. Spoken language is verbal, while e-mail is listed as electronic communication.

qs.q: A client walks to the bathroom with a stooped gait, facial grimacing, and gasping sounds. For which condition should the nurse assess based on these cues?
c: Pain
Anxiety
Depression
Fluid volume deficit
qs.e: The slide's practice example links this cluster of nonverbal cues with assessment for pain. Anxiety is a possible distractor, but it is not the keyed condition for this example.

qs.q: Which forms of communication are classified as electronic in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Social media
E-mail
Text
Snail mail
Paper correspondence
qs.e: Social media, e-mail, and text are electronic forms. Snail mail is listed under paper communication.

qs.q: Self-talk, which the slides note can be very damaging, is _____ communication.
qs.e: Intrapersonal communication is self-talk. Interpersonal communication occurs with two or more people.

qs.q: A nurse and a client exchange information about the client's concerns. Which level of communication is occurring?
c: Intrapersonal
Interpersonal
Self-talk
Paper communication
qs.e: Interpersonal communication involves two or more people. Intrapersonal communication is self-talk rather than an exchange with another person.

qs.q: Which items are included under group communication in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Small-group and organizational communication
Group dynamics, group identity, and cohesiveness
Patterns of interaction, decision making, and responsibility
Leadership and power
Self-talk as the definition of group communication
An absence of interaction patterns
qs.e: The slides include small-group and organizational communication along with these group processes and characteristics. Self-talk belongs to intrapersonal communication.

qs.q: A nurse is considering factors that may influence communication with a client. Which factors are identified in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Developmental level
Gender
Sociocultural differences
Space and territory
Only the spoken words matter
Communication is independent of personal differences
qs.e: Developmental level, gender, sociocultural differences, and space and territory can influence communication. Focusing only on spoken words overlooks these listed factors.

qs.q: Which body areas are specifically listed as private zones? Select all that apply.
c: Head, face, and neck
Mouth
Feet
Front of the body and genitalia
Elbows
Back of the hands
qs.e: The slide lists the head, mouth, feet, face, neck, front of the body, and genitalia as private zones. Elbows and the backs of the hands are not included in that list.

qs.q: A nurse asks about a client's occupation, hobbies, and relationships while considering communication preferences. Which explanation best supports this action?
c: Occupations and hobbies can affect communication preferences, and roles and relationships influence communication
Only developmental level affects communication preferences
Relationships matter only during group communication
Occupation determines whether a client can provide feedback
qs.e: The slides identify roles and relationships as influences and specifically note that occupations and hobbies can affect communication preferences. They do not limit preferences to developmental level.

qs.q: Which additional factors should a nurse consider when evaluating communication with a client? Select all that apply.
c: Physical, mental, and emotional state
Values
Environment
Trust
Only the nurse's intended meaning
The assumption that all clients communicate alike
qs.e: The slides identify the client's state, values, environment, and trust as communication influences. Assuming everyone communicates alike ignores those influences.

qs.q: Which features describe a social relationship? Select all that apply.
c: Mutual exchange between two people with equally shared information
Spontaneous development
Consideration of both friends' needs
No time limits
Unequal sharing of information
A required definitive conclusion
qs.e: Social relationships involve spontaneous, mutual exchange, consideration of both friends' needs, equally shared information, and no time limits. Unequal information sharing and a definitive conclusion characterize the helping relationship.

qs.q: Which features describe a helping relationship? Select all that apply.
c: It is also called a professional relationship
It involves providing and receiving assistance in meeting human needs
It has a specific purpose or goal and a definitive conclusion
Information is shared unequally
It has no time limits
It requires equal attention to both friends' needs
qs.e: The helping relationship is professional, assistance-focused, goal-directed, and has a definitive conclusion with unequal information sharing. Equal consideration of friends' needs and no time limits describe social relationships.

qs.q: According to the slides, how many phases does a helping relationship have?
qs.e: The slides state that a helping relationship has three phases. The supplied slide text does not name those phases.

qs.q: Which dispositional traits are identified as relevant to the nurse's therapeutic relationship? Select all that apply.
c: Warmth and friendliness
Openness
Respect
Empathy
Giving approval of the client's decisions
Projecting personal concerns onto the client
qs.e: Warmth and friendliness, openness, respect, and empathy are listed dispositional traits. Giving approval is listed as nontherapeutic, and projecting personal concerns reflects sympathy rather than empathy.

qs.q: Which additional qualities are included among the nurse's dispositional traits? Select all that apply.
c: Honesty and authenticity
Trustworthiness
Caring
Competence
False reassurance
Defending team members against client concerns
qs.e: The slides identify honesty, authenticity, trustworthiness, caring, and competence as dispositional traits. False reassurance and defending other team members are nontherapeutic techniques.

qs.q: Trying to see things from the patient's point of view is called _____.
qs.e: Empathy keeps the perspective on the patient. Sympathy shifts the perspective toward the nurse's feelings and personal concerns.

qs.q: A nurse shares personal feelings and concerns and projects them onto a client. Which concept does this illustrate?
c: Empathy
Sympathy
Clarifying
Active listening
qs.e: The slides describe sympathy as shifting the perspective away from the patient to the nurse and projecting the nurse's concerns onto the patient. Empathy instead tries to see the situation from the patient's perspective.

qs.q: Which approaches demonstrate therapeutic conversation skills? Select all that apply.
c: Attend to tone of voice and remain flexible during discussion
Be clear and avoid confusing words
Be truthful and keep an open mind
Look for openings in the conversation
Use confusing wording to direct the discussion
Keep the discussion rigid regardless of what the client says
qs.e: Therapeutic conversation includes attention to tone, flexibility, clarity, truthfulness, an open mind, and looking for openings. Rigid discussion and confusing words oppose these skills.

qs.q: Which behaviors demonstrate active listening as described in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Sit with the client
Remain alert
Appear relaxed and natural
Use eye contact when appropriate
Insist on eye contact in every situation
Stop attending when the client pauses
qs.e: Active listening includes sitting, being alert, appearing relaxed and natural, and using eye contact when appropriate. The qualification 'if appropriate' means eye contact is not required in every situation.

qs.q: A client is silent after the provider discusses a diagnosis of epilepsy. Which response is most appropriate?
c: Tell the client the silence is not normal
Allow time to think and explore inner thoughts
Fill the silence with lighter conversation
Ask the provider for a psychiatric referral because of the silence
qs.e: The slide's practice question supports allowing time for thought and inner exploration. Filling the silence removes that opportunity; therapeutic silence also allows clients to speak freely.

qs.q: A nurse is considering therapeutic touch beyond placing a hand on a client's shoulder or hand. According to the slides, what should the nurse do?
c: Ask for consent
Assume consent because the relationship is professional
Replace consent with humor
Use the touch without discussion
qs.e: The slide lists a hand on the shoulder or hand and directs the nurse to ask consent for anything more. A professional relationship does not replace that direction.

qs.q: A nurse considers using humor during a client interaction. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Use humor in every interaction
Assess the situation and use humor appropriately
Use humor whenever the client becomes silent
Use humor instead of discussing feelings
qs.e: The slides advise assessing the situation and using humor appropriately. Humor is not an automatic response to silence or a substitute for discussing feelings.

qs.q: Which nurse question matches the slide's example of an open-ended question about food?
c: What did you have for lunch today?
You ate lunch, right?
Why did you choose that lunch?
Are you having pain right now?
qs.e: The slide explicitly identifies 'What did you have for lunch today?' as open-ended. 'Are you having pain right now?' is identified as validating.

qs.q: A nurse wants to use an open-ended question about the client's current experience. Which statement is most appropriate?
c: You're not really sad, right?
How are you feeling right now?
I think you are making the right choice
Everything happens for a reason
qs.e: The slide lists 'How are you feeling right now?' as an open-ended question. 'You're not really sad, right?' leads the client toward a particular answer.

qs.q: According to the therapeutic-techniques slide, how is the question 'Are you having pain right now?' classified?
c: Validating
Reflective
Giving advice
Exploring
qs.e: The slide explicitly places this pain question under validating questions. Although it can receive a brief answer, the slide classifies this particular example as validating.

qs.q: A nurse says, 'You seem upset, can we talk about it?' Which therapeutic technique does this match in the slides?
c: Validating
Giving approval
False reassurance
Asking why
qs.e: This is a listed validating example. It does not approve a decision or promise that everything will be fine.

qs.q: A client mentions a history of trauma. Which response uses the slide's clarifying technique?
c: You mentioned a history of trauma, can you elaborate on that?
Everything happens for a reason
My grandma had a similar experience
You should stop thinking about it
qs.e: Asking the client to elaborate on a mentioned history is the slide's clarifying example. Sharing a personal story shifts the discussion toward the nurse rather than clarifying the client's meaning.

qs.q: A nurse says, 'Did I understand you correctly when you said you hate coming to the hospital?' Which technique is being used?
c: Clarifying
Defending the health care team
Giving advice
Leading the client
qs.e: The slide identifies this check of understanding as clarifying. Unlike a leading question, it asks whether the nurse understood what the client said.

qs.q: Which question is explicitly listed as a reflective question in the slides?
c: What went well today?
Are you having pain right now?
Why are you upset?
You're not really sad, right?
qs.e: 'What went well today?' is listed as reflective. The pain question is listed as validating, while asking why and leading questions are nontherapeutic.

qs.q: A nurse asks, 'What would you like to accomplish before you're discharged?' How is this question classified in the slides?
c: Reflective
Closed-ended
False reassurance
Giving approval
qs.e: The slide identifies this discharge-focused question as reflective. It asks the client to consider desired accomplishments rather than providing approval of a decision.

qs.q: Which approaches are specifically listed as therapeutic techniques? Select all that apply.
c: Focus on feelings
Provide neutral responses
Tell the client they are wrong
Give approval of the client's choices
Offer false reassurance
qs.e: Focusing on feelings and providing neutral responses are therapeutic techniques. Giving approval and telling the client they are wrong are listed as nontherapeutic.

qs.q: A nurse observes that a client has been crying. Which statement uses the slide's technique of stating observed behaviors?
c: I can see you have been crying
You have nothing to worry about
You're not really sad, right?
I think you are making the right choice
qs.e: The slide uses 'I can see you have been crying' as an example of stating observed behavior. Saying there is nothing to worry about is false reassurance rather than an observation.

qs.q: Which nurse statement is listed as an example of stating observed behavior?
c: Let's talk more about why you're pacing in your room
Sally is actually a fantastic nurse
Everything happens for a reason
My grandma also had cancer
qs.e: The therapeutic-techniques slide explicitly lists the pacing statement under observed behaviors. Despite containing the word 'why,' this specific example is presented as therapeutic; the other options match nontherapeutic examples.

qs.q: A client describes frustration about their health. Which response best reflects, restates, or rephrases the client's message?
c: It sounds like you're frustrated about your health right now
I am sure everything will be fine
You should not feel that way
Let's discuss something else
qs.e: The slide uses this statement as an example of reflecting, restating, or rephrasing. False reassurance does not restate the client's expressed frustration.

qs.q: Which statements are listed as exploring techniques? Select all that apply.
c: Let's talk about it
What is going on in your life that is stressful?
I think you are making the right choice
You're not really sad, right?
Everything happens for a reason
qs.e: The slides list both invitations to discuss the situation or life stress as exploring techniques. Giving approval, leading questions, and clichés are nontherapeutic.

qs.q: Which communication behaviors should the nurse avoid according to the nontherapeutic-techniques slide? Select all that apply.
c: Using closed-ended questions
Forgetting that clients are human
Failing to listen
Telling the client they are wrong
Providing neutral responses
Allowing the client to speak freely
qs.e: The nontherapeutic slide lists closed-ended questions, forgetting clients' humanity, failure to listen, and telling clients they are wrong as behaviors to avoid. Neutral responses and allowing free expression are therapeutic.

qs.q: A nurse asks a client, 'You're not really sad, right?' Which nontherapeutic technique is this?
c: Leading question
Clarifying question
Reflective question
Neutral response
qs.e: The slide identifies this statement as a leading question. It points toward an expected answer rather than neutrally inviting the client's perspective.

qs.q: A client discusses a personal decision. The nurse responds, 'You should choose the option I recommend.' Which nontherapeutic technique does this illustrate?
c: Giving advice
Active listening
Validating
Stating observed behavior
qs.e: Telling the client what to choose is giving advice, which the slides list as nontherapeutic. It is not an observation of the client's behavior.

qs.q: A client discusses having cancer. The nurse responds, 'My grandma also had cancer.' Which nontherapeutic technique does this match?
c: Talking about yourself
Clarifying
Reflecting the client's words
Providing a neutral response
qs.e: The slide uses this exact statement as an example of talking about yourself. It introduces the nurse's personal experience rather than reflecting the client's message.

qs.q: A nurse tells a worried client, 'I am sure everything will be fine. You have nothing to worry about.' Which inappropriate technique is this?
c: False reassurance
Giving advice
Being judgmental
Changing the subject
qs.e: The slide's practice question identifies this statement as false reassurance. It promises a favorable outcome rather than recommending a particular action, so giving advice is not the best answer.

qs.q: The statement 'Everything happens for a reason' is the slide's example of a _____.
qs.e: The slides list this statement as a cliché to avoid. It is not an exploration of the client's individual feelings.

qs.q: A nurse says, 'I think you are making the right choice.' Which nontherapeutic technique does this illustrate?
c: Giving approval
Providing a neutral response
Clarifying
Exploring
qs.e: The slide identifies this statement as giving approval. It expresses the nurse's judgment rather than remaining neutral.

qs.q: The nontherapeutic-techniques slide specifically lists asking '_____' as a behavior to avoid.
qs.e: Asking why is included in the nontherapeutic list. The therapeutic slide instead offers specific examples of open-ended, validating, clarifying, and reflective questions.

qs.q: A client complains about a nurse. The responding nurse says, 'Sally is actually a fantastic nurse. You must have caught her on a bad day.' Which communication technique does the nurse's statement illustrate?
c: Defending other health care team members
Validating the client's concern
Exploring the client's experience
Stating an observed behavior
qs.e: The slide uses this statement as an example of defending other health care team members, which is a nontherapeutic technique. It does not validate or explore the client's concern, nor is it a statement of observed behavior.

qs.q: When using SBAR in its listed order, which component comes first?
qs.e: SBAR follows Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation. Background follows Situation rather than starting the sequence.

qs.q: In SBAR, which component follows Assessment?
qs.e: Recommendation follows Assessment and is the final component in the listed sequence. Background comes before Assessment.

qs.q: Which statements about SBAR are supported by the slides? Select all that apply.
c: It can be used for hand-off communication
It can be used for nurse-to-provider discussions
It is used to improve communication effectiveness
Its sequence is Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
It is limited to communication with clients
Assessment comes before Background
qs.e: SBAR supports effective communication and can be used for hand-offs and nurse-to-provider discussions. Its listed order places Background before Assessment.

qs.q: A client begins discussing a concern, and the nurse redirects the conversation to an unrelated topic. Which nontherapeutic technique is the nurse using?
c: Changing the subject
Exploring
Reflecting
Clarifying
qs.e: Changing the subject is listed as a nontherapeutic technique. Exploring or clarifying would continue examining the client's concern instead of moving away from it.

qs.q: During the communication role-play activity, a student is assigned the narrator role. Which action is part of this role?
c: Acting out the situation using the dialogue and cues
Responding using the assigned therapeutic technique
Introducing each approach and explaining the difference
Demonstrating the assigned communication barrier
qs.e: The narrator introduces each approach and explains the difference between the two nurse responses. Acting out the cues belongs to the patient, and demonstrating the barrier belongs to the nontherapeutic nurse.

qs.q: The instructor is planning the activity for 82 students and wants every group to keep the roles clear. Which grouping structure is recommended?
c: 20 groups of 4 (80 students) plus 1 group of 5
21 groups of 4 (84 students)
10 groups of 8 (80 students) plus 1 group of 2
20 groups of 5 (100 students)
qs.e: The recommended structure is 20 groups of 4 = 80 students and 1 group of 5 = 82 students total. The other options do not match the slide numbers and would blur the four assigned roles.

qs.q: A group has 5 members instead of 4. Which additional role should this group add so the roles stay clear?
c: A second patient
An observer/feedback coach
A second narrator
A timekeeper only
qs.e: In the group of 5, the extra student becomes the observer/feedback coach. A second patient or narrator would duplicate roles the slide assigns once per group.

qs.q: All 21 groups want to present live, which may be too long. What does the instructor suggest?
c: Splitting presentations across stations or sessions
Cutting the debrief time to zero
Having only the therapeutic nurse present
Skipping the nontherapeutic demonstration
qs.e: If all groups present live, the slide suggests splitting presentations across stations or sessions. Removing the debrief or the nontherapeutic demonstration defeats the purpose of comparing the two responses.

qs.q: Time allows after the skits. What should the group do to maximize learning?
c: Rotate roles among group members
Repeat the same scene with the same roles
Watch other groups but not present
Add a second nontherapeutic nurse
qs.e: Rotate roles if time allows so each student practices both therapeutic and nontherapeutic responses. Repeating the same role adds little new practice.

qs.q: A student assigned the nontherapeutic nurse role says they will act 'as mean and dramatic as possible.' Which instruction applies?
c: Demonstrate the assigned communication barrier realistically, not cruelly or theatrically
Make the scene as dramatic as possible to hold attention
Use sarcasm so the contrast is obvious
Ignore the patient's cues to show poor listening
qs.e: The barrier must be shown realistically, not cruelly or theatrically. Overacting turns the scene into a caricature and obscures the actual communication barrier.

qs.q: A student is writing the therapeutic nurse's line on the Dialogue Planner. How should that nurse respond?
c: With medical terminology to sound authoritative
With empathy, respect, and patient-centered language
With a quick answer so the skit stays short
With a joke regardless of the patient's mood
qs.e: The therapeutic nurse responds with empathy, respect, and patient-centered language. Being brief or joking is not required and can override the patient's concern.

qs.q: What must the narrator do first when the skit begins?
c: Introduce the setting and the patient's concern and briefly explain that two different nursing responses will be demonstrated
Explain why the nontherapeutic nurse is wrong before the scene starts
Recite the patient's diagnosis and lab values
Announce the grade the group expects
qs.e: The narrator sets the scene by introducing the setting and patient's concern and noting that two different nursing responses will be shown. Judging the response before it happens spoils the comparison.

qs.q: A client in the emergency department waiting area says, 'I've been waiting for hours... I'm getting really frustrated.' Which therapeutic technique is assigned for this scenario?
c: Reflective question or comment
Exploring statement
Open-ended questions
False reassurance
qs.e: Scenario 1 assigns a reflective question or comment, acknowledging the frustration and inviting the patient to explain the main concern. False reassurance is a nontherapeutic barrier.

qs.q: The angry ED waiting-area patient suddenly says the chest tightness is getting worse. What is the priority action?
c: Assess and escalate the new or worsening symptoms rather than treating the issue as only a complaint
Document the complaint and continue the conversation
Tell the patient the wait will be over soon
Ask the patient to speak to the provider at discharge
qs.e: The clinical note states that new or worsening symptoms must be assessed and escalated, not handled as only a complaint. Continued small talk misses a potential change in condition.

qs.q: Which nurse response in Scenario 1 demonstrates the nontherapeutic barrier of aggressive behavior?
c: 'It sounds like this wait has been really hard. What is your main concern right now?'
Responding with a defensive or confrontational tone that escalates the interaction
Pausing and letting the patient finish the sentence
Reflecting the patient's frustration back to them
qs.e: Aggressive behavior appears as a defensive or confrontational tone that escalates the interaction. Acknowledging and reflecting the frustration are the therapeutic moves.

qs.q: A med-surg client before a routine IV insertion says, 'I'm terrified of needles... Is this going to hurt?' Which therapeutic technique is assigned?
c: Using appropriate, gentle humor
Arguing with the patient's fear
Guaranteeing the stick will not hurt
Telling the patient there is no reason to be afraid
qs.e: Scenario 2 uses appropriate, gentle humor — kept gentle, patient-led, and paired with a real answer to the concern. Arguing or guaranteeing no pain is nontherapeutic.

qs.q: The nurse uses gentle humor with the nervous IV patient, but the client frowns and pulls further away. Which action is appropriate?
c: Stop and use another supportive approach
Push the humor further to break the tension
Tell the patient it was only a joke
Ask the patient to relax and hold still
qs.e: Humor is not appropriate for every patient; if the patient does not respond positively, stop and use another supportive approach. Continuing the humor ignores the patient's reaction.

qs.q: Which statement by the nurse demonstrates the nontherapeutic barrier of arguing in Scenario 2?
c: Pairs gentle, patient-led humor with a real answer about the needle
Debates the fear or tells the patient there is no reason to be afraid
Acknowledges the fear and explains what will happen
Asks the patient what would make the procedure easier
qs.e: Arguing means debating the fear or insisting there is no reason to be afraid, which dismisses the patient's experience. The other options answer the concern and support the patient.

qs.q: A hospitalized client says quietly, 'Sometimes I wonder if there's any point in trying anymore.' Which therapeutic technique is assigned, and what does the nurse say?
c: Exploring statement: invite the patient to say more about what 'no point' means to them
Changing the subject to the plan of care
Telling the client that many patients feel this way and it passes
Asking the client to focus on the positive
qs.e: Scenario 3 uses an exploring statement to invite the patient to explain what 'no point' means to them. Changing the subject or minimizing is the nontherapeutic failure to listen.

qs.q: After the client expresses hopelessness, which action does the clinical note require?
c: Listen directly and assess for thoughts of self-harm or suicide when indicated, following protocol and notifying the appropriate team
Wait for the provider to ask the client about mood
Assume the client is simply tired from the hospital stay
Ask another visitor to stay with the client
qs.e: Hopelessness may signal a safety concern, so the nurse listens directly and assesses for self-harm or suicide thoughts when indicated, per protocol, and notifies the team. Assuming fatigue ignores a potential safety risk.

qs.q: Which nurse behavior shows the nontherapeutic barrier of failure to listen in Scenario 3?
c: Looking distracted, changing the subject, or responding without attending to the concern
Pausing before answering and waiting for the patient
Inviting the patient to say more about 'no point'
Speaking quietly and matching the patient's pace
qs.e: Failure to listen looks distracted and shifts the subject instead of attending to the concern. Pausing and inviting more detail are therapeutic behaviors.

qs.q: After the provider explains a new diagnosis, a client says, 'I'm not sure what that means for me. Can you help me understand what happens next?' Which technique is assigned?
c: Open-ended questions
Accusatory 'why' questions
Closed yes/no questions
Repeating the full discharge talk word for word
qs.e: Scenario 4 assigns open-ended questions to learn what the patient understood and what needs clarifying. Accusatory 'why' questions imply blame and shut down the conversation.

qs.q: The client asks the nurse exactly what the new kidney diagnosis means for life expectancy. What is the most appropriate response?
c: Explain within the nurse's role using plain language and contact the provider for questions requiring medical clarification
Give the client the provider's personal phone number
Explain using medical terminology so the client can research it
Tell the client the provider will explain everything at discharge
qs.e: The nurse explains within the nursing role in plain language and contacts the provider for questions needing medical clarification. Answering prognosis questions or handing out personal contact information exceeds the nurse's role.

qs.q: Which nurse statement shows the nontherapeutic barrier of accusatory 'why' questions?
c: Asking, 'Why weren't you listening?' when the client looks uncertain
Asking, 'What have you understood so far about your kidneys?'
Using plain language to describe the plan
Offering to clarify what the client most wants to know
qs.e: 'Why weren't you listening?' is an accusatory why question that implies blame. The open, plain-language options invite the patient to share what they understood.

qs.q: A preoperative client keeps asking, 'What if something goes wrong while I'm asleep?' Which therapeutic technique is assigned?
c: Offering realistic reassurance and support
False reassurance or promises
Guaranteeing that nothing bad will happen
Telling the client surgery is routine so there is no risk
qs.e: Scenario 5 uses realistic reassurance and support — acknowledging the fear and offering to find answers. Promising an outcome is the nontherapeutic barrier of false reassurance.

qs.q: The preoperative client asks the nurse exactly how long the surgeon will take. What is the most appropriate action?
c: Do not promise an outcome and refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate member of the surgical team
Give the client the surgeon's best estimate to reduce anxiety
Guarantee the procedure will be routine and quick
Ask the client to sign the consent and stop worrying
qs.e: The clinical note says not to promise an outcome and to refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate surgical team member. Estimates and guarantees are false reassurance.

qs.q: Which response demonstrates the nontherapeutic barrier of false reassurance or promises?
c: The nurse guarantees that nothing bad will happen
The nurse acknowledges the fear and explains what the team can do
The nurse offers to find answers to specific questions
The nurse asks what the client is most worried about
qs.e: False reassurance is promising that nothing bad will happen. Acknowledging fear, explaining the team's role, and offering to find answers are the therapeutic actions.

qs.q: A client at a hypertension follow-up says, 'I'm tired of taking pills every day... I'm just worn out.' Which action best fits the assigned therapeutic technique?
c: Listen without interrupting and reflect the burden the client describes
Suggest a new diet plan immediately
Tell the client that many people live with high blood pressure
Remind the client that nonadherence causes problems
qs.e: Scenario 6 uses active listening — listening without interrupting and reflecting the burden described. Jumping to teaching or reminding about consequences skips over the client's experience.

qs.q: Which nurse statement shows the nontherapeutic barrier of judgmental comments in Scenario 6?
c: 'It must be exhausting to take pills every day and change what you eat.'
'You would feel better if you just tried harder.'
'What part of the changes feels the hardest?'
'Tell me more about what is wearing you out.'
qs.e: 'You would feel better if you just tried harder' judges the client's effort, which is the assigned nontherapeutic barrier. Reflecting burden and asking for more detail are therapeutic.

qs.q: Which roles are assigned in each group for this therapeutic and nontherapeutic role-play? Select all that apply.
c: Patient
Therapeutic nurse
Nontherapeutic nurse
Narrator
Observer/feedback coach
Unit secretary
qs.e: Every group assigns a patient, therapeutic nurse, nontherapeutic nurse, and narrator. The observer/feedback coach is added only to the single group of 5, and a unit secretary is not one of the activity roles.

qs.q: Which expectations apply when students build their skit? Select all that apply.
c: Create your own dialogue; the scenario is a starting point
Keep the interaction realistic and respectful
Use course materials to support your choices
End by explaining why one response is therapeutic and the other is not
Memorize the scenario dialogue word for word
Make the scene as dramatic as possible
qs.e: Students write their own dialogue, keep it realistic and respectful, support choices with course materials, and close by explaining the difference. Word-for-word memorization and over-dramatizing contradict the instructions.

qs.q: Which timing suggestions are given for the activity? Select all that apply.
c: Group preparation: 8–10 minutes
Skits: 2–3 minutes each
Debrief: 1 minute per skit
Group preparation: 30 minutes
Skits: 10 minutes each
Debrief: 5 minutes per skit
qs.e: The slide recommends 8–10 minutes to prepare, 2–3 minutes per skit, and a 1-minute debrief per skit. The longer times would make the activity unmanageable with 21 groups.

qs.q: Which fields appear in the Role Assignments section of the Student Dialogue Planner? Select all that apply.
c: Narrator
Patient
Therapeutic nurse
Nontherapeutic nurse
Observer/feedback coach
Charge nurse
qs.e: The planner's role assignments list narrator, patient, therapeutic nurse, and nontherapeutic nurse. Observer/feedback coach belongs to the group-of-5 structure, not the planner's role lines.

qs.q: Which narrator responsibilities are described in the Student Dialogue Planner? Select all that apply.
c: Introduce the setting and the patient's concern
Briefly explain that two different nursing responses will be demonstrated
Explain why the therapeutic response worked
Explain why the nontherapeutic response was ineffective
Deliver the nurse's therapeutic dialogue
Demonstrate the communication barrier
qs.e: The narrator sets the scene and then explains and wraps up why one response worked and the other did not. The nurse lines belong to the therapeutic and nontherapeutic nurses.

qs.q: Which elements should the patient include in a follow-up response during rehearsal? Select all that apply.
c: Words
Tone
Facial expression
Body language
Vital signs
Laboratory results
qs.e: The patient's follow-up response includes words, tone, facial expression, and body language. Vital signs and lab results are not part of the acting cues for this activity.

qs.q: Which items are on the rehearsal Final Check? Select all that apply.
c: Both nurses responded to the same patient concern
The assigned techniques are clear
The scene is realistic and respectful
The narrator explains why the responses differ
The skit is at least 5 minutes long
A full reference list is submitted
qs.e: The four check boxes confirm the same patient concern, clear assigned techniques, a realistic and respectful scene, and the narrator's explanation. Skit length and references are not check box items.

qs.q: Which patient acting cues belong to Scenario 1 (the angry ED waiting-area patient)? Select all that apply.
c: Speak sharply
Glance toward the desk
Interrupt once
The patient is upset but not threatening
Cry uncontrollably
Refuse all contact
qs.e: The cues are speaking sharply, glancing toward the desk, and interrupting once — upset but not threatening. Uncontrolled crying or refusing contact would change the scenario the group is assigned.

qs.q: Which instructions apply when using humor as the therapeutic technique in Scenario 2? Select all that apply.
c: Keep the humor gentle
Let the humor be patient-led
Pair the humor with a real answer to the concern
Stop and use another supportive approach if the patient does not respond positively
Use sarcasm to lighten the mood
Continue the humor even if the patient withdraws
qs.e: Humor must be gentle, patient-led, and paired with a real answer, and it stops if the patient does not respond positively. Sarcasm or pushing through a negative reaction is not therapeutic.

qs.q: Which behaviors demonstrate the nontherapeutic barrier of failure to listen in Scenario 3? Select all that apply.
c: Looking distracted
Changing the subject
Responding without attending to the concern
Pausing before answering
Speaking quietly
Avoiding eye contact
qs.e: Looking distracted, changing the subject, and responding without attending are the failure-to-listen behaviors. Pausing, quiet speech, and avoiding eye contact are the patient's acting cues, not the nurse's barrier.

qs.q: Which nurse actions belong to the therapeutic response in Scenario 5 (preoperative anxiety)? Select all that apply.
c: Acknowledge the fear
Explain what the team can do
Offer to find answers to specific questions
Do not promise an outcome
Guarantee that nothing bad will happen
Refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate surgical team member
qs.e: The nurse acknowledges the fear, explains the team's role, offers to find answers, avoids promising outcomes, and refers procedure questions to the surgical team. Guaranteeing nothing bad will happen is the nontherapeutic barrier.

qs.q: Which patient acting cues belong to Scenario 6 (the frustrated hypertension client)? Select all that apply.
c: Fold your arms
Sound frustrated rather than indifferent
Speak sharply and interrupt once
Pull your arm close to your body
Pause before answering
Fidget with the blanket
qs.e: Scenario 6 cues are folding the arms and sounding frustrated rather than indifferent. The sharp interruptions, arm pulling, pausing, and blanket fidgeting are cues from other scenarios.

qs.q: Which are the therapeutic techniques assigned across the six scenarios? Select all that apply.
c: Reflective question or comment
Using appropriate, gentle humor
Exploring statement
Open-ended questions
Offering realistic reassurance and support
Active listening
qs.e: Each scenario pairs one therapeutic technique: reflection (1), gentle humor (2), exploring (3), open-ended questions (4), realistic reassurance (5), and active listening (6).

qs.q: Which are the nontherapeutic barriers assigned across the six scenarios? Select all that apply.
c: Aggressive behavior
Arguing
Failure to listen
Accusatory 'why' questions
False reassurance or promises
Judgmental comments
qs.e: The six barriers map one-to-one to scenarios 1–6. None of these match the therapeutic technique paired with the same scenario.

qs.q: How many distinct scenarios does this communication activity include?
qs.e: Slide 1 lists 20 distinct scenarios covering patient-centered communication and clinical judgment.

qs.q: The recommended grouping for 82 students totals how many students in groups of 4?
qs.e: 20 groups of 4 = 80 students, with the remaining 2 students placed in one group of 5.

qs.q: How many minutes are suggested for group preparation?
qs.e: Group preparation is timed at 8–10 minutes, long enough to write dialogue but short enough for 21 groups.

qs.q: Each skit should run approximately how many minutes?
qs.e: Skits run 2–3 minutes each; longer skits would crowd out other groups and the debrief.

qs.q: How many minutes of debrief are suggested per skit?
qs.e: Debrief is 1 minute per skit — just enough for the narrator to explain the difference between the two responses.

qs.q: In which setting does Scenario 1 take place?
qs.e: Scenario 1 is the angry patient in the emergency department waiting area, a long-wait complaint setting.

qs.q: What nontherapeutic barrier is assigned to Scenario 1?
qs.e: Scenario 1 pairs the reflective question or comment with the nontherapeutic barrier of aggressive behavior.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 2 (the IV start)?
qs.e: Scenario 2 uses appropriate, gentle humor, which must still be paired with a real answer to the patient's fear.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 3 (the client expressing hopelessness)?
qs.e: Scenario 3 uses an exploring statement to find out what 'no point' means to this patient.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 4 (the client who does not understand the plan)?
qs.e: Scenario 4 uses open-ended questions; the nontherapeutic counterpart is accusatory 'why' questions.

qs.q: What therapeutic technique is assigned to Scenario 5 (the anxious preoperative client)?
qs.e: Scenario 5 uses realistic reassurance and support, never a promise about the outcome.

qs.q: What chronic condition is the focus of the Scenario 6 follow-up visit?
qs.e: Scenario 6 is a hypertension follow-up visit where the client is worn out by pills and diet changes.

qs.q: At what point must the Student Dialogue Planner be completed?
qs.e: The Dialogue Planner is to be completed before rehearsal so the group can build and refine its dialogue (Slide 4 footer: COMPLETE BEFORE REHEARSAL).

qs.q: A client says, “I know my blood pressure is high, but I’m worn out from pills and changing everything I eat.” Which response best demonstrates active listening?
c: “You need to be more responsible.”
“Taking pills and changing your eating habits have become exhausting for you.”
“Let me explain your options before you say more.”
“You are choosing to be noncompliant.”
qs.e: Reflecting the burden and listening without interrupting demonstrate active listening. Labeling the client or moving to options before hearing the concern does not.

qs.q: Which nurse statements are judgmental responses to the client who is tired of managing high blood pressure? Select all that apply.
c: “You are being lazy.”
“You are irresponsible about your health.”
“You are just noncompliant.”
“What makes taking your pills difficult?”
“Changing your eating habits sounds burdensome.”
qs.e: Lazy, irresponsible, and noncompliant are the labels identified as nontherapeutic. Exploring difficulty and reflecting burden avoid those judgments.

qs.q: Before discussing options with the care team, which barriers should the nurse explore with this client? Select all that apply.
c: Medication cost
Side effects
Daily routines
Food access
Whether the client deserves a label of noncompliance
qs.e: The clinical note specifically identifies cost, side effects, routines, and food access as barriers to explore. Assigning a judgmental label is not barrier assessment.

qs.q: A student portrays the client who feels worn out by blood pressure management. Which performance follows the acting cues?
c: Fold the arms and sound frustrated.
Remain indifferent and unconcerned.
Become tearful and silently hold a tissue.
Brace the abdomen before standing.
qs.e: This role calls for folded arms and frustration rather than indifference. The other physical cues belong to different scenarios.

qs.q: The designated therapeutic technique for the client exhausted by blood pressure management is ______.
qs.e: Active listening includes hearing the client without interruption and reflecting the burden. Immediately discussing options skips the exploration emphasized in this scenario.

qs.q: After her mother's death, a family member says, “I don’t know how I’m supposed to go home without her.” Which response is most appropriate?
c: “Everything happens for a reason.”
“What kind of support would feel helpful right now?”
“Let me tell you about my own loss.”
“You need to feel better before going home.”
qs.e: Asking what support would help offers emotional support without assumptions. A stock phrase such as “Everything happens for a reason” is a cliché.

qs.q: Which actions support therapeutic communication with the grieving family member? Select all that apply.
c: Ask what support would feel helpful.
When appropriate, ask about spiritual practices that matter to the family.
When appropriate, ask about cultural practices that matter to the family.
Assume the family's beliefs from their appearance.
Try to make the grief feel better immediately.
qs.e: Support should be guided by the family's expressed needs and relevant spiritual or cultural practices. The slide warns against assuming beliefs or trying to resolve grief immediately.

qs.q: Which response to a grieving family member requires follow-up?
c: “What support would help you?”
“Are there cultural practices that matter to your family?”
“Everything happens for a reason.”
“Would you like to tell me what matters to you right now?”
qs.e: “Everything happens for a reason” is the slide's example of a nontherapeutic cliché. Individualized questions about support do not impose a stock explanation for the loss.

qs.q: Which acting cues belong to the grieving family member role? Select all that apply.
c: Become tearful.
Pause.
Hold a tissue without speaking for a moment.
Check a phone and shrug.
Attempt to stand while looking frightened.
qs.e: Tearfulness, pauses, and silently holding a tissue portray this grieving family member. Looking frightened while attempting to stand belongs to the newly confused client scenario.

qs.q: Complete the designated technique: Offering emotional or ______ support.
qs.e: The technique is offering emotional or spiritual support. Spiritual support should not be based on assumptions about the family's beliefs.

qs.q: A client is newly confused after a procedure and asks, “Where am I?” Which response follows the demonstrated reorientation sequence?
c: Offer a next step, then leave without explanation.
Introduce yourself, calmly explain where the client is and why, and offer a simple next step.
Tell the client not to worry and discuss options later.
Ask the client to stop being silly before introducing yourself.
qs.e: The demonstrated sequence is introduction, calm explanation of place and reason, then a simple next step. Minimizing the concern does not reorient the client.

qs.q: A client develops new confusion after a procedure. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Assess the new confusion.
Report it promptly.
Protect the client from falls.
Assume it is a normal part of aging.
Tell the client the concern is silly.
qs.e: New confusion requires assessment, prompt reporting, and fall protection. It must not be dismissed as normal aging.

qs.q: Which statement minimizes the concerns of a frightened, confused client?
c: “I am your nurse.”
“You are in the hospital after your procedure.”
“Let me explain a simple next step.”
“You are being silly; there is nothing to worry about.”
qs.e: Calling the client silly or saying there is nothing to worry about minimizes the concern. Calmly explaining the situation presents reality instead.

qs.q: Which cues are specified for the newly confused older client? Select all that apply.
c: Look around the room.
Attempt to stand.
Appear frightened.
Pull sleeves over the hands.
Present an already-final decision about treatment.
qs.e: The role includes looking around, attempting to stand, and appearing frightened. Pulling sleeves over the hands belongs to the body image scenario.

qs.q: Complete the technique for the newly confused client: Presenting reality and ______.
qs.e: Presenting reality and reorientation address the client's uncertainty about the situation. Reassuring the client that nothing is wrong does not replace assessment of new confusion.

qs.q: A hospitalized adolescent says, “My friends barely text me anymore. I think they’ve forgotten about me.” Which response best uses mirroring?
c: “It sounds like you feel forgotten by your friends.”
“This is just teen drama.”
“You should stop checking your phone.”
“Your concern is not important right now.”
qs.e: Mirroring reflects the central feeling or meaning and allows the adolescent to respond. Dismissing the concern as teen drama is specifically discouraged.

qs.q: Which nurse behaviors demonstrate nonverbal boredom in the isolated adolescent scenario? Select all that apply.
c: Sighing
Checking a phone
Looking at the clock
Appearing uninterested
Reflecting the adolescent's central feeling
Allowing the adolescent to respond
qs.e: The slide lists sighing, checking a phone, looking at the clock, and appearing uninterested as nontherapeutic cues. Reflecting meaning and allowing a response are therapeutic.

qs.q: Which action is most appropriate when discussing the adolescent's isolation from friends?
c: Dismiss it as teen drama.
Maintain privacy and speak respectfully.
Reflect the feeling but do not allow a response.
Check the time repeatedly while listening.
qs.e: The clinical note emphasizes privacy and respectful communication. Reflecting a feeling without allowing the adolescent to respond is incomplete mirroring.

qs.q: Which acting sequence is specified for the isolated adolescent?
c: Look at the phone, place it face down, and shrug.
Reach toward the nurse, then hesitate.
Brace the abdomen and hesitate before standing.
Fold the arms and sound frustrated about pills.
qs.e: Looking at the phone, putting it face down, and shrugging are the assigned cues. Reaching toward the nurse belongs to the client afraid of dying.

qs.q: The isolated adolescent scenario pairs restating with the equivalent technique of ______.
qs.e: Restating or mirroring reflects the central feeling or meaning. It is not an opportunity to replace the adolescent's concern with advice.

qs.q: After difficult chemotherapy cycles, a client says, “I’m not sure it’s worth it.” Which response is most appropriate?
c: “You cannot give up now.”
“What does ‘not worth it’ mean to you, and what matters most right now?”
“I will consider your decision final.”
“You should be ashamed of stopping.”
qs.e: Clarification explores the client's meaning and current priorities. The scenario does not present the decision as already final.

qs.q: Which responses are disapproving communication toward the client questioning chemotherapy? Select all that apply.
c: Scolding the client
Shaming the client
Implying that the client is giving up
Asking what matters most now
Clarifying what “not worth it” means
qs.e: Scolding, shaming, and implying that the client is giving up are the specified nontherapeutic behaviors. Clarifying values and meaning supports understanding instead.

qs.q: Which actions follow the clinical note for a client considering whether to continue chemotherapy? Select all that apply.
c: Support informed decision-making.
Avoid pressuring the client.
Communicate concerns and questions to the oncology team.
Treat uncertainty as a final refusal.
Shame the client into continuing.
qs.e: The nurse supports informed decisions without pressure and shares concerns and questions with the oncology team. Uncertainty should not be converted into a final decision.

qs.q: Which portrayal follows the acting cues for the client questioning chemotherapy?
c: Speak slowly, appear tired, and remain uncertain about the decision.
Speak forcefully and present the decision as final.
Act indifferent to the side effects.
Focus only on friends not sending messages.
qs.e: The client should speak slowly and appear tired without presenting a final decision. Portraying a settled refusal changes the scenario's intended uncertainty.

qs.q: The designated therapeutic technique for exploring what a client means by chemotherapy being “not worth it” is a ______.
qs.e: A clarifying statement explores meaning and what matters most to the client. A disapproving comment instead scolds or shames.

qs.q: A new parent says, “I barely sleep, and I’m scared I won’t know what to do at home.” Which response best validates the feeling?
c: “This transition sounds difficult, and you are feeling scared.”
“You should follow my advice before discussing your worries.”
“Your fear means you are not a good parent.”
“There is nothing difficult about this transition.”
qs.e: Validation recognizes the difficulty and the feeling without judging parenting ability. Immediately directing the parent without listening is the nontherapeutic approach in this scenario.

qs.q: Which nurse action demonstrates the nontherapeutic use of advice in the overwhelmed-parent scenario?
c: Listening to the parent's concerns first
Recognizing the difficulty of the transition
Immediately telling the parent what to do without listening
Acknowledging fear without judging ability
qs.e: The specified problem is immediately telling the parent what to do before listening. Recognizing the difficult transition is validation, not premature advice.

qs.q: Which reports from the new parent require a serious response and appropriate assessment and escalation? Select all that apply.
c: Feeling unsafe
Being unable to care for themselves
Being unable to care for the baby
Having thoughts of harm
Asking for help without knowing exactly what to request
qs.e: The clinical note identifies feeling unsafe, inability to care for self or baby, and thoughts of harm as escalation concerns. An unclear request for help is an acting cue, not one of those specifically listed triggers.

qs.q: Which performance follows the overwhelmed new parent's acting cues?
c: Look tired, speak softly, and ask for help without knowing exactly what to request.
Speak loudly and claim no help is needed.
Look at a phone, place it face down, and shrug.
Insist pain is zero while guarding an incision.
qs.e: The cues emphasize fatigue, soft speech, and an uncertain request for help. Guarding an incision despite denying pain belongs to another scenario.

qs.q: Recognizing a new parent's difficult transition and feelings without judging ability demonstrates a ______.
qs.e: A validating statement acknowledges the parent's experience. It does not judge parenting ability or replace listening with immediate advice.

qs.q: A postoperative client says pain limits getting out of bed. Which question is neutral and focused?
c: “It’s not that bad, is it?”
“You can move without much pain, correct?”
“Where does it hurt when you try to get out of bed?”
“You are exaggerating, aren't you?”
qs.e: Asking where the pain occurs neutrally explores its location. Questions that suggest an expected answer are leading rather than focused assessment.

qs.q: Which pain dimensions are specifically suggested for neutral questions in this scenario? Select all that apply.
c: Location
Severity
Timing
Effect on movement
Whether the client agrees the pain is not bad
qs.e: The slide names location, severity, timing, and effect on movement. Seeking agreement that pain is not bad embeds an expected answer.

qs.q: Which actions follow the clinical note for unexpected postoperative pain? Select all that apply.
c: Assess pain.
Assess associated symptoms.
Follow the care plan.
Report concerning changes.
Assume pain is an expected complication.
qs.e: Pain and associated symptoms require assessment, with care-plan follow-through and reporting of concerning changes. The slide explicitly warns against assuming pain is an expected complication.

qs.q: Which acting cues portray the postoperative client whose pain limits movement?
c: Brace the abdomen when shifting and hesitate before standing.
Hold a tissue silently after becoming tearful.
Watch the nurse's reaction while answering cautiously.
Avoid eye contact and cover the hands with sleeves.
