qs.q: Which assessments are included as vital signs in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Temperature and pulse
Respirations and blood pressure
Pulse oximetry
Pain level
Appetite
Muscle coordination
qs.e: The slides identify temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and pain level as vital signs that reflect physiologic functioning and health status. Appetite and coordination appear elsewhere as symptoms, not as listed vital signs.

qs.q: Which situations require assessment of vital signs? Select all that apply.
c: Admission to a health care facility
A scheduled assessment required by facility policy
A change in condition or loss of consciousness
A report of changed status, pain, or distress
Only when an invasive procedure is planned
Only when the client has a fever
qs.e: Admission, facility policy, changes in condition, loss of consciousness, and reported changes or distress are all indications for assessment. Vital signs are not reserved for fever or invasive procedures.

qs.q: The nurse is planning care for a client undergoing an invasive diagnostic procedure and later ambulating after surgery. When should vital signs be assessed?
c: Only after the diagnostic procedure
Before and after both the procedure and the potentially risky activity
Only before the first postoperative ambulation
Only if the client reports pain
qs.e: Assess vital signs before and after surgical or invasive diagnostic procedures and activities that may increase risk, such as ambulation after surgery. Waiting for pain alone misses the scheduled assessment indications.

qs.q: The nurse is preparing to administer a medication that affects cardiovascular and respiratory function. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Assess vital signs before administering the medication
Assess vital signs only if the client loses consciousness
Wait until the next routine assessment regardless of medication timing
Assess pain instead of cardiovascular and respiratory vital signs
qs.e: The slides require vital sign assessment before medications that affect cardiovascular and respiratory function. A routine assessment schedule does not replace this medication-related indication.

qs.q: Which structure controls thermoregulation by conserving body heat or increasing heat loss?
qs.e: The hypothalamus controls thermoregulation. Body temperature reflects the difference between heat produced by the body and heat lost to the environment.

qs.q: Which factors affect body temperature according to the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Time of day
Biologic sex and age
Physical activity and state of health
Environmental temperature
Blood pressure cuff width
Blood pressure cuff looseness
qs.e: The listed temperature factors are time of day, biologic sex, age, physical activity, health status, and environmental temperature. Cuff width and looseness affect blood pressure readings rather than being listed temperature factors.

qs.q: Which locations are identified as core body temperature locations? Select all that apply.
c: Intracranial
Intrathoracic
Intra-abdominal
Axillary
Posterior sublingual pocket
qs.e: The slides list intracranial, intrathoracic, and intra-abdominal locations as core locations. Axillary and sublingual sites are assessment sites, not members of this listed core-location group.

qs.q: According to the slides, body tissues and cells function best within what temperature range in degrees Celsius?
qs.e: The stated optimal range is 36°C to 37.5°C. The slide also includes 98.6°F parenthetically, but does not provide a complete Fahrenheit range.

qs.q: A client asks why temperature measurements vary during the day. Which response reflects the circadian pattern in the slides?
c: Temperature is highest in the morning and lowest from 1500 to 1800
Temperature remains constant throughout the day
Temperature is lower in the morning and peaks from 1500 to 1800
Temperature peaks only during physical activity
qs.e: Circadian rhythm produces predictable temperature fluctuations, with lower readings in the morning and a peak between 1500 and 1800. The reverse pattern is not the pattern described.

qs.q: Which statement by a student indicates understanding of environmental effects on temperature?
c: Extreme cold may lead to hyperthermia
Extreme heat may lead to hypothermia
Environmental temperatures do not affect body temperature
Extreme cold may lead to hypothermia, and extreme heat may lead to hyperthermia
qs.e: Extreme cold may cause hypothermia, while extreme heat may cause hyperthermia. Reversing these relationships misidentifies the environmental risks.

qs.q: What term describes a client who does not have a fever?
qs.e: Afebrile means without fever. Pyrexia means fever, and a client with an increased temperature is described as febrile.

qs.q: Which interpretation of an elevated temperature matches the slides?
c: A temperature above 40°C is not dangerous unless pain is present
A temperature above 40°C (>104°F) is dangerous, and 41°C (106°F) or higher is a medical emergency
Only temperatures below 40°C are considered hyperpyrexia
A temperature of 41°C requires no more concern than the usual tissue-function range
qs.e: The slides identify temperatures above 40°C as dangerous and temperatures at or above 41°C as a medical emergency called hyperpyrexia. Pain is not required for these temperature thresholds to be concerning.

qs.q: Which findings are listed signs or symptoms of fever? Select all that apply.
c: Loss of appetite
Headache and thirst
Hot, dry skin
Muscle aches and fatigue
Slurred speech and amnesia
Decreased respirations, heart rate, and blood pressure
qs.e: Fever findings include loss of appetite, headache, hot dry skin, thirst, muscle aches, and fatigue. Slurred speech, amnesia, and decreased vital signs are listed under hypothermia instead.

qs.q: A febrile client needs comfort measures before medication administration. Which nonpharmaceutical measures are listed in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: A cool bath
Cooling blankets
Removing excess clothing and blankets
Oral fluids to prevent dehydration
An antipyretic
A Bair Hugger to promote warmth
qs.e: Cool baths, cooling blankets, removal of excess coverings, and oral fluids are listed nonpharmaceutical fever measures. An antipyretic is pharmaceutical, while a Bair Hugger is listed for hypothermia.

qs.q: Which statement best explains the purpose of treating pyrexia?
c: Fever has no role in the immune response
Treatment is intended only to change the documented number
Fever is an immune defense response, but treatment promotes comfort and prevents complications
Antipyretics are nonpharmaceutical comfort measures
qs.e: Fever is an important immune defense mechanism, but treatment aims to provide comfort and prevent complications. The slides identify antipyretics under pharmaceutical treatment, not nonpharmaceutical care.

qs.q: Which findings are listed manifestations of hypothermia? Select all that apply.
c: Poor coordination and slurred speech
Amnesia
Hallucinations and stupor
Decreased respirations, heart rate, and blood pressure
Increased respirations, heart rate, and blood pressure
Hot, dry skin with thirst
qs.e: Hypothermia findings include coordination and speech changes, amnesia, hallucinations, stupor, and decreased respirations, heart rate, and blood pressure. Hot dry skin and thirst are listed with fever.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with hypothermia. Which plan matches the slides?
c: Use cooling blankets and remove excess clothing
Use warm blankets, warm fluids, and a Bair Hugger to promote warmth
Provide a cool bath and an antipyretic
Avoid warming measures until the client reports thirst
qs.e: Hypothermia treatment aims to raise body temperature and promote warmth using warm blankets, warm fluids, and a Bair Hugger. Cooling measures belong to pyrexia management.

qs.q: Which thermometer types or attachments appear in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Infrared
Tympanic
Electronic oral/axillary
Rectal electronic attachment
Pulse oximeter
Blood pressure cuff
qs.e: The thermometer slide lists infrared, tympanic, electronic oral/axillary, and a rectal electronic attachment. A pulse oximeter and blood pressure cuff assess different vital signs.

qs.q: Where should the nurse place an oral thermometer according to the slides?
c: In the center of the axilla
Against the outside of the cheek
In the posterior sublingual pocket under the tongue
Between the front teeth
qs.e: Oral placement is in the posterior sublingual pocket under the tongue, described as close to the carotid artery. The center of the axilla is the placement site for an axillary temperature.

qs.q: Which conditions or precautions apply to oral temperature measurement? Select all that apply.
c: The client must be awake and alert
No hot or cold drinks for 20 minutes beforehand
No smoking for 20 minutes beforehand
Avoid the oral route in small children because they may bite down
The oral route is appropriate for an unconscious client
Recent cold drinks do not affect preparation
qs.e: Oral measurement requires an awake, alert client and avoidance of hot or cold drinks and smoking for 20 minutes. The slides advise against oral measurement in small children because of biting.

qs.q: According to the slides, how many minutes should an oral thermometer remain in place?
qs.e: The stated oral measurement time is 3 minutes. The 5–10-minute interval applies to axillary measurement instead.

qs.q: Which statement demonstrates correct understanding of axillary temperature measurement?
c: Place the bulb in the center of the axilla and lower the arm across the chest; this noninvasive route is good for children but less accurate
Place the bulb under the tongue and keep the arm extended
The axillary route is more accurate because major vessels are nearby
An axillary temperature measures 0.5°C higher than an oral temperature
qs.e: Axillary placement uses the center of the axilla with the arm lowered across the chest; it is noninvasive but less accurate because no major vessels are nearby. The slide states that axillary temperature measures 0.5°C lower, not higher, than oral temperature.

qs.q: According to the slides, how many minutes should an axillary thermometer remain in place?
qs.e: The axillary measurement interval is 5–10 minutes. The shorter 2–3-second interval belongs to the ear route.

qs.q: An unconscious adult needs a temperature assessment, and the nurse selects the rectal route described in the slides. Which technique is correct?
c: Keep the client upright and insert an unlubricated bulb
Position the client side-lying with the upper leg flexed and insert the lubricated bulb 1–1½ inches
Place the bulb in the posterior sublingual pocket
Position the client side-lying with both legs straight and insert the bulb only into the axilla
qs.e: The slides describe rectal measurement when oral measurement is unsafe or inaccurate, including unconscious, disoriented, or irrational clients. Adult technique uses side-lying positioning, an upper flexed leg, lubrication, and insertion of 1–1½ inches.

qs.q: Which combination correctly describes rectal temperature measurement in the slides?
c: Leave in place 5–10 minutes; expect 0.5°C lower than oral
Leave in place 2–3 seconds; expect the same as axillary
Leave in place 2–3 minutes; expect 0.5°C higher than oral
Leave in place 3 minutes; expect 0.5°C lower than oral
qs.e: The rectal measurement interval is 2–3 minutes, and the reading is described as 0.5°C higher than oral. The lower reading and 5–10-minute interval describe axillary measurement.

qs.q: Which statements about ear temperature assessment match the slides? Select all that apply.
c: For an adult, pull the pinna up and back
The site is close to the hypothalamus and sensitive to core temperature changes
Measurement is rapid and the site is easily accessible
Cerumen impaction and otitis media can distort readings
Cerumen impaction improves measurement accuracy
Leave the thermometer in place for 5–10 minutes
qs.e: The ear route is rapid, accessible, and sensitive to core temperature changes; adult positioning uses the pinna up and back. Cerumen impaction and otitis media distort rather than improve the reading.

qs.q: How many seconds does ear temperature measurement take according to the slides?
qs.e: The stated ear measurement time is 2–3 seconds. Rectal measurement uses a similar numerical interval but is measured in minutes.

qs.q: Which explanation correctly describes how a palpable pulse is produced and detected?
c: Left ventricular contraction sends a blood wave through arteries, which can be felt by lightly pressing an artery against underlying bone or muscle
Expiration sends a blood wave through the skin, requiring firm thumb pressure
The pulse is generated only during ventricular relaxation
Pulse assessment measures the amount of air inhaled and exhaled
qs.e: Left ventricular contraction produces a wave of blood through the arteries. Light palpation against underlying bone or muscle detects that wave; respiratory depth measures air movement instead.

qs.q: Which groups contain only pulse sites listed in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Carotid and brachial
Radial and femoral
Popliteal and posterior tibial
Dorsalis pedis
Posterior sublingual pocket
Intrathoracic and intra-abdominal
qs.e: The listed pulse sites are carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis. The sublingual pocket and core locations belong to temperature content.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe pulse assessment? Select all that apply.
c: Assess rate
Assess rhythm
Assess amplitude
Pulse assessment can use palpation and auscultation
Rhythm describes only how full the pulse feels
Amplitude means the number of breaths per minute
qs.e: Pulse assessment includes rate, rhythm, and amplitude and may use palpation or auscultation. Rhythm concerns the beat pattern, whereas amplitude concerns pulse volume.

qs.q: Which action by a student assessing a peripheral pulse requires correction?
c: Using the second finger
Using the third or fourth finger
Placing fingers lightly where an artery passes over bone
Using the thumb to palpate the pulse
qs.e: The slides direct the nurse to use the second, third, or fourth fingers lightly and not to use the thumb. Light finger placement over an artery and underlying bone follows the stated technique.

qs.q: The nurse detects an irregular radial pulse. Which counting sequence follows the slides?
c: Count 30 seconds and multiply by 2 without further assessment
Count the radial pulse for 1 minute, then the apical pulse for a full minute
Count the apical pulse for 15 seconds, then stop
Count the radial pulse for 2–3 seconds, then assess temperature
qs.e: For an irregular pulse, count the radial pulse for 1 minute and then the apical pulse for a full minute. Counting 30 seconds and multiplying by 2 is the routine approach before the irregularity exception.

qs.q: Which approach correctly assesses the apical pulse?
c: Palpate the radial artery for 30 seconds
Observe chest movement for one minute
Auscultate at the heart's apex or PMI for a full minute, listening to the 'Lub-Dub'
Palpate the carotid artery with the thumb
qs.e: The apical pulse is the heartbeat at the apex or PMI and is auscultated for a full minute. Peripheral pulses are palpated rather than assessed using this apical technique.

qs.q: What adult pulse-rate range, in beats/minute, is listed in the slides?
qs.e: The listed pulse range is 60–100 beats/minute, with an average of 80 beats/minute. The 12–20 range belongs to adult respirations.

qs.q: Which documentation correctly uses pulse rhythm and amplitude terminology?
c: Rhythm regular; amplitude weak or thready because the pulse lacks fullness
Rhythm bounding because the beats occur at regular intervals
Amplitude imperceptible because pulse volume is higher than normal
Amplitude full and bounding because the pulse cannot be felt or heard
qs.e: Rhythm describes a regular or irregular beat pattern; amplitude is the volume pushed against the arterial wall during ventricular contraction. Weak or thready lacks fullness, full or bounding has higher-than-normal volume, and imperceptible cannot be felt or heard.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe respiratory physiology? Select all that apply.
c: Respiration involves gas exchange between oxygen and carbon dioxide
Respiration has autonomic and voluntary components
Inspiration means inhalation or breathing in
Expiration means exhalation or breathing out
Inspiration means breathing out
Respiration is exclusively voluntary
qs.e: Respiration exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide and has both autonomic and voluntary components. Inspiration is breathing in, not breathing out.

qs.q: The nurse has just assessed a client's pulse. Which action is most appropriate when assessing respirations?
c: Release the hand and ask the client to deliberately change breathing
Continue holding the client's hand and observe respiratory rate, rhythm, and depth without making the counting apparent
Assess only the number of breaths and omit rhythm and depth
Ask the client to count each breath aloud
qs.e: The slides recommend observing respirations after the pulse while still holding the client's hand so the client is unaware of the count. Assessment includes rate, rhythm, and depth, not rate alone.

qs.q: What is the normal adult respiratory rate in breaths/minute?
qs.e: The normal adult respiratory rate is 12–20 breaths/minute. One inhalation and one exhalation together count as one breathing cycle.

qs.q: Which set of respiratory documentation terms is correctly matched?
c: Tachypnea: decreased rate; bradypnea: increased rate; apnea: labored breathing
Tachypnea: increased rate; bradypnea: decreased rate; apnea: absence of breathing
Tachypnea: absent breathing; bradypnea: normal breathing; apnea: rapid breathing
Tachypnea: shallow depth only; bradypnea: deep breathing; apnea: regular rhythm
qs.e: Tachypnea is an abnormal increase in respiratory rate, bradypnea is an abnormal decrease, and apnea is absence of breathing. Difficult or labored breathing is dyspnea, not apnea.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes respiratory depth and shortness of breath as presented in the slides?
c: Depth is the regularity of pauses, and shallow breathing has large chest movements
Depth is the amount of air inhaled and exhaled; normal movements are deep and even, shallow movements are minimal, and SOB is described as shallow and rapid
Depth is the number of pulse beats, and SOB means no breathing
Shallow breathing and deep, even chest movement describe the same finding
qs.e: Depth refers to the amount of air inhaled and exhaled, with minimal chest rise and fall indicating shallow breathing. Rhythm concerns regularity, while the slides describe shortness of breath as shallow and rapid.

qs.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes respiratory rhythm from character?
c: Normal rhythm has very little variation in pauses between inhalation and exhalation; dyspnea describes difficult or labored breathing
Rhythm is the amount of air inhaled; dyspnea means no breathing
Normal rhythm requires widely varying pauses; character is the pulse amplitude
Character describes only the number of breathing cycles per minute
qs.e: Rhythm is the regularity of inhalation and exhalation, with little variation in normal pauses. Character concerns departures from normal effortless breathing, including dyspnea; absence of breathing is apnea.

qs.q: Which explanation of blood pressure is accurate?
c: Blood pressure is force against vessel walls; systolic is the highest pressure during contraction, and diastolic is the lowest pressure during relaxation
Blood pressure is respiratory depth; systolic occurs only during inhalation
Systolic is the lowest pressure during relaxation, and diastolic is the highest during contraction
Blood pressure measures only the volume of air exhaled
qs.e: Blood pressure is the force blood exerts against vessel walls. Systolic is the highest pressure during contraction, while diastolic is the lowest during relaxation, not the reverse.

qs.q: Which groups contain factors affecting blood pressure that are listed in the slides? Select all that apply.
c: Position changes and drugs or medications
Food and exercise
Age and weight
Biological sex, race, and stress
Cerumen impaction and otitis media
Thick nail polish and pulse oximeter probe rotation
qs.e: The listed blood pressure factors include position, medications, food, exercise, age, weight, biological sex, race, and stress. Cerumen and otitis media concern ear temperature readings, while nail polish and probe rotation concern pulse oximetry.

qs.q: When considering blood pressure effects of position changes in an older adult, which condition do the slides identify as common?
c: Hyperpyrexia
Orthostatic hypotension
Apnea
Otitis media
qs.e: The slides identify orthostatic hypotension as common in older adults under the topic of position changes. Hyperpyrexia is a severe temperature elevation, not the listed position-related concern.

qs.q: Which interpretation follows the blood pressure values in the slides?
c: Normal is less than 120/80; hypotension is systolic below 90 mmHg or diastolic below 60 mmHg
Normal is greater than 140/90; hypotension requires both values to exceed normal
Normal is 130–139/80–89; hypotension is systolic above 180
Normal is exactly 120/80; hypotension requires a temperature change
qs.e: The slides define normal blood pressure as less than 120/80 and hypotension as systolic below 90 or diastolic below 60 mmHg. The hypotension wording uses 'or,' so it does not require both values to be below their thresholds.

qs.q: Which blood pressure category descriptions reproduce the slide values? Select all that apply.
c: Prehypertension (elevated): systolic 120–129 and diastolic 80
Hypertension stage 1: systolic 130–139, diastolic 80–89
Hypertension stage 2: systolic greater than 140, diastolic greater than 90
Prehypertension: systolic below 90 or diastolic below 60
Hypertension stage 1: less than 120/80
Hypertension stage 2: systolic 120–129 and diastolic 80
qs.e: These three correct descriptions use the slide's stated category values. Below 90 systolic or 60 diastolic describes hypotension, while less than 120/80 is listed as normal. ⚠ Her cheat sheet (memorize it per the FAQ) differs: elevated = 120–129 and diastolic LESS than 80; Stage 2 = 140+/90+; crisis = over 180 / over 120.

qs.q: Complete the threshold exactly as presented in the slides: Hypertensive crisis is greater than _____ mmHg.
qs.e: The slide lists hypertensive crisis as greater than 180. It does not provide an additional diastolic crisis threshold. ⚠ Her cheat sheet (memorize it per the FAQ) differs: elevated = 120–129 and diastolic LESS than 80; Stage 2 = 140+/90+; crisis = over 180 / over 120.

qs.q: According to the slides, the blood pressure cuff should cover what percentage of the arm circumference?
qs.e: The slide states that the cuff should cover 40% of arm circumference and the bladder should cover two-thirds of the arm. Cuff size is judged by arm circumference, not age.

qs.q: Which statements correctly describe blood pressure positioning or measurement errors? Select all that apply.
c: Support the arm at heart level with the palm upward
An arm above heart level causes a falsely low reading
A cuff that is too wide causes a falsely low reading
A cuff that is too narrow or too loose causes a falsely high reading
An arm above heart level causes a falsely high reading
A cuff that is too loose causes a falsely low reading
qs.e: The arm should be supported at heart level with the palm upward. Above-heart positioning and an overly wide cuff produce falsely low readings, whereas an overly narrow or loose cuff produces falsely high readings.

qs.q: The nurse listens while gradually releasing pressure from a blood pressure cuff. What are the sounds heard as blood flows through the previously occluded artery called?
c: Apical sounds
Korotkoff sounds
Respiratory cycles
Circadian fluctuations
qs.e: Korotkoff sounds occur as blood flows through an artery after cuff occlusion while cuff pressure is gradually released. Apical assessment instead involves listening to the heartbeat at the apex.

qs.q: Which group consists entirely of limb alerts listed for blood pressure assessment?
c: PICC line, arteriovenous fistula, and the arm on the side of a mastectomy
Cerumen impaction, otitis media, and recent cold drinks
Thick nail polish, thirst, and headache
An alert client, an upward-facing palm, and a supported arm
qs.e: The slide lists PICC lines, AV fistulas, and the arm on the side of a mastectomy as limb alerts. Ear conditions and recent drinks relate to temperature assessment rather than these blood pressure limb alerts.

qs.q: A client asks what pulse oximetry measures. Which response matches the slides?
c: It invasively measures blood pressure
It noninvasively calculates SpO2, providing a reliable estimate of arterial oxygen saturation
It measures only respiratory depth
It directly measures core body temperature
qs.e: Pulse oximetry is a noninvasive measurement that calculates SpO2 as a reliable estimate of arterial oxygen saturation. It does not replace measurement of respiratory depth, blood pressure, or temperature.

qs.q: Complete the pulse oximetry probe-site list from the slides: finger, ear, nose, and _____.
qs.e: The listed probe sites are the finger, ear, nose, and toe. The posterior sublingual pocket is an oral temperature site, not a listed pulse oximetry site.

qs.q: Which actions follow the slide recommendations for pulse oximetry? Select all that apply.
c: Remove thick nail polish
Wait until the readout reaches a constant value and the pulse display reaches full strength
Routinely inspect skin beneath the probe during continuous monitoring
Rotate the probe during continuous monitoring
Document the first fluctuating value without waiting
Leave the probe at the same site without skin checks
qs.e: The slides recommend removing thick nail polish, waiting for a stable value and full-strength pulse display, and inspecting skin and rotating the probe during continuous monitoring. An unstable initial value and neglected skin checks do not follow these instructions.

qs.q: For which client does the slide identify the PQRST pain scale as appropriate?
c: A client who is verbal and aware
A client who is unconscious
A client who cannot communicate verbally and is unaware
Only a client with hyperpyrexia
qs.e: The slide identifies PQRST for verbal, aware patients. It does not identify unconscious clients as the intended group or restrict the scale to clients with fever.

qs.q: Vital signs may reveal ______ changes in a client's condition in addition to changes that occur progressively over time.
qs.e: The slide states vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition as well as changes that occur progressively over time. Both patterns matter because a client can deteriorate quickly or drift slowly.

qs.q: A ______ set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the client's condition.
qs.e: A baseline set of vital signs gives you a comparison point, which is how you identify change. Without a baseline, a single set of numbers cannot show whether the client's condition has changed.

qs.q: A client's normal ______ can be different from our standard values.
qs.e: The slide asks whether a client's normal range can differ from standard values; the teaching point is that it can. Judging a client only against standard values ignores individual variation.

qs.q: Based upon assessment information, the nurse identifies and prioritizes the top ______ client problems related to vital signs.
qs.e: The learning objective is to identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs based on assessment information. Prioritization, not a simple list of all findings, is the goal.

qs.q: Because the client has an increased respiratory rate, the nurse conducts further assessment to determine if ______ is adequate.
qs.e: The objective directs the nurse to assess for adequate oxygenation when the respiratory rate is increased. An increased rate alone does not tell you whether oxygenation is adequate.

qs.q: The nurse is reviewing a client's vital signs and compares them with the values obtained on admission. Which statement best explains why this baseline set of vital signs is important?
c: It provides a comparison point used to identify changes in the client's condition
It confirms that the client's values match standard values exactly
It means vital signs do not need to be reassessed later in the shift
It allows the nurse to report the numbers without any other considerations
qs.e: A baseline set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the client's condition. It is not a one-time event; vital signs may reveal sudden changes as well as progressive changes, so reassessment is still needed.

qs.q: A client's temperature and heart rate have climbed a little more with each assessment over the past 3 days. This trend best illustrates that vital signs may reveal:
c: Changes that occur progressively over time
Sudden changes in a client's condition
A baseline set of vital signs
Standard values that apply to every client
qs.e: The slide distinguishes changes that occur progressively over time from sudden changes. A steady upward trend across assessments is progressive change, not an abrupt change.

qs.q: At 0700 a client's vital signs were within normal limits. At 0800 the client is newly confused with a heart rate of 132. This finding best demonstrates that vital signs may reveal:
c: Sudden changes in a client's condition
Changes that occur progressively over time only
That a baseline set is not needed
That standard values replace individual assessment
qs.e: Vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition in addition to changes that occur progressively over time. The rapid change between two assessments is the sudden pattern.

qs.q: A student nurse reports a client's vital signs as numbers only. The instructor says the student has not addressed vital sign considerations. Which statement by the student indicates understanding?
c: When assessing vital signs, I must take into consideration factors besides the numbers
The numbers alone are all I need to determine a client's condition
Standard values are the same for every client without exception
Once I have a baseline, I only compare numbers to standard values
qs.e: The slide explicitly prompts the nurse to consider what else, besides numbers, should be taken into consideration when assessing vital signs. Reporting numbers alone ignores that consideration and ignores individual normal range.

qs.q: A client asks, 'Are my vital signs normal?' The client's values differ slightly from standard values but are the same as the values the client usually has. Which response by the nurse is correct?
c: A client's normal range can be different from our standard values, and we compare your values with your usual values as well
Any value that differs from standard values is abnormal and must be reported
Standard values apply to every client without exception
Only the numbers matter, so no other factors are considered
qs.e: The slide asks whether a client's normal range can be different from our standard values, and the point is that it can. Answering with standard values alone would ignore the client's individual normal range.

qs.q: The nurse is determining whether a client's vital signs are within normal limits. Which action is most appropriate?
c: Compare the client's values with normal limits while also considering the client's individual normal range
Assume the standard values apply to the client without question
Compare only the numbers with standard values and consider nothing else
Wait to see whether the values change progressively over time before judging them
qs.e: The objective is to determine whether vital signs are within normal limits, and the slide notes that a client's normal range can differ from standard values. Considering only standard values or only numbers omits vital sign considerations.

qs.q: After assessing a client's vital signs and other assessment information, which action best meets the learning objective for this client?
c: Identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs
List every vital sign value in the chart without prioritizing
Report the numbers and let the provider identify the problems
Identify only the single most abnormal vital sign
qs.e: The objective is to use assessment information to identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs. Reporting numbers alone or limiting analysis to one problem does not meet that objective.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose health status has changed. Which question should guide the nurse's analysis of this change?
c: What is the source of the change in the client's health status?
Are the vital signs identical to standard values?
Should the vital signs be reported as numbers only?
Can the assessment be postponed until the next baseline is obtained?
qs.e: The objective directs the nurse to determine the source of the change in health status. Comparing values only with standard values does not identify the source of the change.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with an elevated temperature, and medication has been ordered. Which nursing action comes first?
c: Implement interventions to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration
Withhold all interventions and wait for the medication to take effect
Report the temperature as a number only
Compare the temperature with standard values and take no further action
qs.e: The objective asks what interventions the nurse can take to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration. Waiting for the medication alone ignores nursing interventions that can assist before it is given.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with an increased respiratory rate. Which additional assessment is indicated?
c: Determine whether the client has adequate oxygenation
Compare the respiratory rate with standard values only
Report the respiratory rate as a number only
Wait for the rate to change progressively over time
qs.e: The objective asks what other assessment should be conducted to determine if the client has adequate oxygenation when the respiratory rate is increased. The rate alone does not establish that oxygenation is adequate.

qs.q: A student nurse makes the following statement about vital signs. Which statement is correct?
c: A client's normal range can be different from our standard values
Standard values apply to every client without exception
Only the numbers should be considered when assessing vital signs
A baseline set of vital signs is needed only for clients who are unstable
qs.e: The slide states that a client's normal range can be different from standard values. The slide also asks what else besides numbers to consider, so numbers alone are not sufficient.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose vital signs are unchanged from the client's own baseline but differ from standard values. The nurse should:
c: Recognize that the client's normal range can be different from standard values and continue to compare with the client's baseline
Report the client as abnormal because the values differ from standard values
Take no further action because the numbers are unchanged from the baseline
Consider only the numbers and no other factors
qs.e: A client's normal range can be different from our standard values, so comparison with the client's own baseline matters. However, the nurse still considers factors besides numbers rather than stopping at the numbers alone.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client. Which finding requires follow-up in the student's documentation of vital signs?
c: Only the vital sign numbers are documented, with no other considerations
The vital signs are compared with the client's baseline values
The vital signs are described in relation to whether they are within normal limits
Sudden changes in the client's condition are noted in the record
qs.e: The slide asks what else, besides numbers, should be taken into consideration when assessing vital signs. Documenting numbers only omits those considerations and the comparison needed to identify changes in condition.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose condition is changing. Which action by the nurse demonstrates use of a baseline set of vital signs?
c: Comparing today's vital signs with the client's previously obtained vital signs to identify changes in condition
Comparing today's vital signs only with standard values for all clients
Documenting the numbers without comparing them with anything
Waiting for the values to change progressively before comparing them
qs.e: A baseline set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the client's condition, which requires comparison with the client's own previous values. Comparing only with standard values ignores the client's individual normal range.

qs.q: The nurse has completed an assessment. Which action best reflects the idea that vital signs reveal changes over time?
c: Trend today's values with previous values, recognizing both sudden and progressive changes
Record today's values and discard previous values
Use standard values as the only comparison point
Assume that unchanged numbers mean the client's condition is unchanged
qs.e: Vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition in addition to changes that occur progressively over time, so trending values is essential. Discarding previous values removes the comparison needed to see change.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client whose vital signs are being assessed. Which action is most appropriate when determining whether the client's condition is within normal limits?
c: Consider the numbers along with other factors, including the client's own normal range
Use standard values as the only measure of normal for this client
Consider the numbers only and no other factors
Wait for a change to occur before deciding whether the values are normal
qs.e: The slide prompts the nurse to consider what else besides numbers to take into account and notes that a client's normal range can differ from standard values. Using standard values or numbers alone contradicts both points.

qs.q: Which of the following statements about vital signs are accurate? Select all that apply.
c: Vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition
Vital signs may reveal changes that occur progressively over time
Only the client's most recent set of numbers is needed to describe the client's condition
A baseline set of vital signs helps identify changes in the client's condition
Standard values apply to every client without exception
Numbers alone are sufficient to describe a client's condition
qs.e: The slide states that vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition as well as changes that occur progressively over time, and that a baseline set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the patient's condition. The slide rejects the idea that numbers alone are enough and notes that a client's normal range may differ from standard values.

qs.q: The nurse is discussing vital sign considerations with a student. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
c: A client's normal range can be different from our standard values
A baseline set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the client's condition
Vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition
The numbers alone are all that must be taken into consideration
Standard values apply to every client without exception
Vital signs reveal only changes that occur progressively over time
qs.e: The slide supports individual normal range, the value of a baseline, and sudden changes in condition. It also asks what else besides numbers to consider and distinguishes sudden from progressive change, so the last three options are wrong.

qs.q: The nurse is caring for a client with a change in health status, an elevated temperature, and an increased respiratory rate. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
c: Based upon assessment information, identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs
Determine the source of the change in the client's health status
Implement interventions to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration
Conduct further assessment to determine if oxygenation is adequate when the respiratory rate is increased
Assume the client's values are within normal limits without comparison
Report only the vital sign numbers with no other considerations
qs.e: All four reflect the stated learning objectives for this client: identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs, determine the source of the change in health status, implement interventions to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration, and further assess whether oxygenation is adequate with the increased respiratory rate. Assuming values are within normal limits without comparison, or reporting numbers only, omits the baseline comparison and vital sign considerations the slide requires.

qs.q: The nurse is planning care for a client with altered vital signs, including an elevated temperature and an increased respiratory rate. Which questions guide the nurse's analysis? Select all that apply.
c: What is the source of the change in the client's health status?
What interventions can assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration?
What other assessment should be conducted to determine if oxygenation is adequate with an increased respiratory rate?
Can a client's normal range be different from our standard values?
Are standard values identical for every client without exception?
Should vital signs be reported as numbers with no other considerations?
qs.e: These four questions come directly from the objectives (source of the change in health status, temperature interventions prior to medication, and oxygenation assessment with an increased respiratory rate) and from the slide's vital sign considerations. The last two contradict the slide, which states that a client's normal range can differ from standard values and prompts consideration of factors besides numbers.

qs.q: A student is preparing to assess a client's vital signs. Which considerations should the student include? Select all that apply.
c: Factors besides the numbers when assessing vital signs
Whether the client's normal range differs from our standard values
Comparison with the client's baseline set of vital signs
Awareness that vital signs may reveal sudden as well as progressive changes
Only the numbers, because nothing else is taken into consideration
The assumption that standard values apply to every client without exception
qs.e: All four are supported by the slide's vital sign considerations and its statement about baseline and about sudden versus progressive change. Considering numbers only, or applying standard values to everyone, contradicts the slide.

qs.q: The nurse is documenting a client's vital signs. Which statements about vital signs and baseline sets are correct? Select all that apply.
c: A baseline set of vital signs is important to identify changes in the client's condition
Vital signs may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition
Vital signs may reveal changes that occur progressively over time
A baseline set is used to judge every client against standard values only
Once a baseline is obtained, reassessment is unnecessary
qs.e: A baseline set of vital signs identifies change, and that change may be sudden or progressive. The slide does not support judging clients only by standard values, and it does not support abandoning reassessment.

qs.q: A client's vital signs differ from standard values. Which statements should guide the nurse? Select all that apply.
c: A client's normal range can be different from our standard values
Factors besides the numbers are taken into consideration when assessing vital signs
Comparison with the client's baseline set of vital signs helps identify changes
Standard values apply to every client without exception
The numbers alone are all that must be considered
A single set of vital signs is sufficient to identify changes in condition
qs.e: The slide supports individual normal range, consideration beyond the numbers, and the use of a baseline to identify change. Standard values are not the sole measure, numbers alone are not sufficient, and one set without comparison cannot show change.

qs.q: Per her cheat sheet, normal blood pressure is less than ___ mmHg.
qs.e: Normal BP is less than 120/80.

qs.q: A client's BP is 88/58. How does her cheat sheet classify this?
c: Hypotension
Normal
Elevated
Stage 1
qs.e: Hypotension = below 90 systolic or below 60 diastolic. 88/58 meets both.

qs.q: A client's BP is 92/56. How is this classified on her cheat sheet?
c: Normal, because systolic is above 90
Hypotension, because diastolic is below 60
Elevated
Cannot classify without a recheck
qs.e: Hypotension is below 90 systolic OR below 60 diastolic, so one low number is enough.

qs.q: A client's BP is 124/76. Per her cheat sheet this is:
c: Normal
Elevated (prehypertension)
Stage 1
Stage 2
qs.e: Elevated = 120–129 systolic AND less than 80 diastolic.

qs.q: A client's BP is 124/82. Using her cheat sheet, which category fits?
c: Elevated
Stage 1
Normal
Stage 2
qs.e: Elevated requires diastolic less than 80. A diastolic of 80–89 is Stage 1. ⚠ Her Slide 20 says elevated diastolic "of 80," but the cheat sheet (which the FAQ says to memorize) says less than 80.

qs.q: A client's BP is 134/78. How is it classified?
c: Elevated
Stage 1
Stage 2
Normal
qs.e: Stage 1 = 130–139 systolic or 80–89 diastolic. Systolic 134 is Stage 1.

qs.q: A client's BP is 140/90. Per her cheat sheet:
c: Stage 1
Stage 2
Hypertensive crisis
Elevated
qs.e: Stage 2 = 140+/90+, which includes exactly 140/90. ⚠ Slide 20 writes ">140, >90"; the cheat sheet includes 140/90.

qs.q: A client's BP is 186/124. Per her cheat sheet this is:
c: Stage 2
Hypertensive crisis, an emergency
Stage 1
Elevated
qs.e: Hypertensive crisis = over 180 / over 120, labeled an emergency.

qs.q: Hypertensive crisis on her cheat sheet: over 180 systolic / over ___ diastolic.
qs.e: Crisis = over 180 / over 120. Slide 20 gives only ">180."

qs.q: Which BP readings are Stage 2 on her cheat sheet? Select all that apply.
qs.e: Stage 2 = 140+ systolic or 90+ diastolic. 138/88 is Stage 1; 126/68 is Elevated.

qs.q: Elevated (prehypertension) systolic range on her cheat sheet: ___ mmHg.
qs.e: Elevated = 120–129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic.

qs.q: High BP Stage 1 on her cheat sheet: 130–139 / ___ .
Normal temperature range on her cheat sheet: 96.4°F to ___ °F.
qs.e: Normal 96.4–100.4°F ("37°C = heaven"). ⚠ Slide 5 says cells work best at 36–37.5°C (98.6°F).

qs.q: A client's oral temp is 100.8°F. Per her cheat sheet this is:
c: Normal
Fever (pyrexia)
Hyperthermia
Hyperpyrexia
qs.e: Fever = over 100.4°F (38°C).

Report → Assess → Verify

Verify → Report → Reassess in 4 hours

Incorrect positioning
Patient factors

cards.def: The study of how the body moves and aligns during activity; applies ergonomic principles to prevent musculoskeletal injury during everyday activities.
Optimal musculoskeletal balance and operation so that no undue strain is placed on the joints, muscles, tendons, or ligaments.

A state in which the center of gravity is close to its base of support and the object has a wide base of support. Body balance increases when people spread the feet apart and flex the hips and knees, decreasing musculoskeletal strain.
The point of the body or an object where mass is concentrated; keeping it close to the base of support maintains balance and reduces strain.
The area beneath an object or person (formed by the feet) that determines stability; widening it increases balance.
Muscles working together for purposeful movement, using major and stronger muscle groups.
Reflexes that maintain body position and equilibrium during rest or movement; include sensory organs in the inner ear, vision, and autonomic contractions.
Self-care activities that maintain quality of life, such as eating, bathing, dressing, and toileting.
Movement and alignment change from infant through older adult; nurses promote neuromuscular development and facilitate each patient's use of the body to perform self-care activities.

Postural abnormalities (hip dysplasia, torticollis, scoliosis), bone/muscle disorders (dwarfism, osteoporosis, muscular dystrophy), joint/bone mobility issues (arthritis, trauma), and CNS disorders (stroke, spinal cord injury) affect movement.
Depression affects activity level, posture, and energy for ADLs; lifestyle factors include diet, sedentary vs active habits, smoking, and cultural values regarding movement and exercise.
The practice of designing equipment and work tasks to conform to the capability of the worker; provides a means for adjusting the work environment and work practices to prevent injuries.

Applying ergonomics to patient care; proper body movement during all everyday activities (moving a medication cart, pushing a bed, reaching to silence an alarm) helps develop good musculoskeletal habits.
Develop a habit of erect posture with correct alignment; listed first among the applications of ergonomics to prevent injury.
Use the longest and strongest muscles of arms and legs for maximum power; back muscles are weaker and prone to injury when used improperly.
Engage core muscles to stabilize the pelvis and protect the abdomen; contract the gluteal muscles downward and the abdominal muscles upward.
Work as closely to an object as possible to keep the body's center of gravity close to the object being moved, permitting most of the burden to be borne by the legs and arms rather than the back.
Face the direction of your movement; do not twist your body.
Push rather than pull when possible; keep arms close and push with your whole body.
Spread feet shoulder width apart and flex the knees to broaden the base of support.

Assess the patient's ability to assist with planned movement: ability to understand instruction and cooperate, medical diagnosis and health issues, movement capabilities, apply braces/devices, and encourage the patient to assist within capabilities to promote independence.
Ensure enough staff are available to safely move the patient; assess the area for clutter, accessibility, and availability of devices, removing any obstacles or barriers.

cards.term: Safe handling Steps 4–6: Screening, equipment, planning
cards.def: Use a screening or assessment tool; decide which equipment to use; plan carefully and communicate to care team members and the patient.

cards.term: Safe handling Steps 7–9: Pain, bed, wheels
cards.def: Administer prescribed analgesic if the patient is in pain prior to movement; elevate the bed as necessary; lock wheels.
Ensure patient safety during transfer: avoid friction on skin, support the body properly (good alignment, avoid grabbing), and move in a smooth, rhythmic motion.

Causes include uncoordinated lifts, high exertion in awkward positions, manual lifting without assistive devices, repetitive movements, lifting while fatigued, standing for long periods, and transferring/repositioning dependent, cognitively impaired, or obese patients who cannot actively participate.
A device placed under a patient to reduce friction and ease movement during repositioning or transfers.
A belt secured around a patient's waist to assist with standing and ambulation, giving the nurse a safe grasp point.
A device used to help move a patient laterally (side to side) in bed or between surfaces with less effort and risk.
A mechanical lifting device that supports the patient's full body weight to transfer safely between bed, chair, or other surfaces.
A device that helps a patient move from sitting to standing, reducing the effort required by the nurse.
Skills practiced include turning the patient in bed, moving a patient up in bed, moving from bed to gurney, moving from bed to chair, dangling a patient, and ambulating a patient.
The process of exchanging information and generating and transmitting meanings between two or more people.
Initiates information in the communication process.
Actual communication product from the source; can be visual, auditory, or kinesthetic.
How the information is sent (audio, visual, kinesthetic).
Person to whom the message is sent in the communication process.
Response the receiver sends back to the sender in the communication process.
Spoken communication reliant on language.
Body language including touch, eye contact, facial expressions, posture, gait, gestures, physical appearance, dress/grooming, sounds, and silence.
If the verbal and non-verbal messages conflict, the non-verbal message is believed.
Self-talk with oneself; can be very damaging.
Communication with two or more people.
Involves small-group and organizational communication with group dynamics, group identity, cohesiveness, patterns of interaction, decision making, responsibility, leadership, and power.

Developmental level, gender, sociocultural differences, space and territory, roles and relationships, occupations/hobbies (can impact communication preference), physical/mental/emotional state, values, environment, and trust.
Head, mouth, feet, face, neck, front of body, and genitalia are considered private zones in space and territory.
Mutual exchange between two people that occurs spontaneously; needs of both friends are heard and considered with no time limits and equally shared information.
Exists among people who provide and receive assistance in meeting human needs; is goal-directed, has a definitive conclusion, and involves unequal sharing of information.
A helping relationship consists of three phases; it occurs for a specific purpose/goal (goal-directed) and has a definitive conclusion. (The slide text does not name the individual phases.)
Warmth and friendliness, openness, respect, empathy, honesty, authenticity, trustworthiness, caring, and competence are dispositional traits for therapeutic relationships.
Trying to see things from the patient's point of view.
Shifts the perspective away from the patient to the nurse; the nurse shares feelings and personal concerns which are then projected onto the patient.
Tone of voice, flexible with discussion, be clear, avoid confusing words, truthful, open mind, and look for openings.
Sit, be alert, relaxed, natural, and use eye contact if appropriate.
Allow the client to speak freely; when a patient is silent, allow time to think and explore inner thoughts.
Hand on the shoulder or hand is acceptable; anything more requires asking for consent.
Assess the situation and use humor appropriately.
Questions that allow expansive answers, e.g., 'What did you have for lunch today?' 'How are you feeling right now?'
Questions to check understanding or confirm feelings, e.g., 'Are you having pain right now?' 'You seem upset, can we talk about it?'
Questions to confirm or expand on what was said, e.g., 'You mentioned a history of trauma, can you elaborate on that?' 'Did I understand you correctly?'
Focus on feelings; state observed behaviors, reflect/restate/rephrase what the patient said, and provide neutral responses, e.g., 'It sounds like you're frustrated about your health right now.'
Encourage the patient to talk more, e.g., 'Let's talk about it.' 'What is going on in your life that is stressful?'

Techniques to avoid include forgetting they are human, closed-ended questions, failure to listen, leading questions, giving advice, changing the subject, talking about yourself, telling the patient they are wrong, false reassurance, cliches, giving approval, asking why, and defending other health care team members.
An inappropriate technique, e.g., 'I am sure everything will be fine. You have nothing to worry about.'
Non-therapeutic technique that suggests a desired answer, e.g., 'You're not really sad, right?'
Non-therapeutic technique using meaningless comforting phrases, e.g., 'Everything happens for a reason.'
Nursing communication tool standing for Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation; used to improve effectiveness of communication in hand-off and nurse-to-provider discussions.
Situation → Background → Assessment → Recommendation.
Communication is directly linked to establishing and sustaining a healthy work environment; provides safety and quality care.
Nurse responses that use patient-centered techniques (empathy, respect, assigned therapeutic technique) to support the patient and facilitate understanding.
Nurse responses that demonstrate a communication barrier (e.g., arguing, judgment), which escalate or shut down the interaction.
Four roles are assigned: patient (acts out the situation with cues), therapeutic nurse, nontherapeutic nurse, and narrator (introduces each approach and explains the difference).
Introduces the setting and patient's concern, briefly explains that two different nursing responses will be demonstrated, then explains and wraps up why one response is therapeutic.
Uses the patient statement from the assigned scenario and adds realistic emotions, body language, and follow-up lines.
Uses the assigned therapeutic technique and responds with empathy, respect, and patient-centered language.
Demonstrates the assigned communication barrier realistically (not cruelly or theatrically).
A fifth role added in the single group of 5 when 82 students are divided into 20 groups of 4 plus 1 group of 5.
20 groups of 4 = 80 students, plus 1 group of 5 = 82 students total; roles should be rotated if time allows.
Group preparation: 8–10 minutes; skits: 2–3 minutes each; debrief: 1 minute per skit.
Sequence: (1) narrator sets the scene, (2) patient gives opening and cues, (3) therapeutic nurse responds, (4) nontherapeutic nurse demonstrates the barrier, (5) narrator explains and wraps up.
Include words, tone, facial expression, and body language showing how the patient responds to each nurse.
Confirm: both nurses responded to the same patient concern; assigned techniques are clear; scene is realistic and respectful; narrator explains why responses differ.
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the patient's frustration and invites the patient to explain the main concern (Scenario 1).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse escalates the interaction with a defensive or confrontational tone (Scenario 1).
Therapeutic technique kept gentle, patient-led, and paired with a real answer to the concern (Scenario 2).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse debates the patient's fear or tells the patient there is no reason to be afraid (Scenario 2).
Therapeutic technique that invites the patient to say more about what a statement (e.g., 'no point') means to them (Scenario 3).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse looks distracted, changes the subject, or responds without attending to the concern (Scenario 3).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse asks 'Why weren't you listening?' or otherwise implies blame (Scenario 4).
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the fear, explains what the team can do, and offers to find answers to specific questions (Scenario 5).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse guarantees that nothing bad will happen (Scenario 5).
Therapeutic technique: listen without interrupting and reflect the burden the patient describes (Scenario 6).
Nontherapeutic barrier in which the nurse makes critical or evaluative remarks toward the patient (Scenario 6).
If the patient reports new or worsening symptoms, the nurse should assess and escalate them rather than treating the issue as only a complaint.
Humor is not appropriate for every patient; if the patient does not respond positively, stop and use another supportive approach.

Hopelessness may signal a safety concern; the nurse should listen directly and assess for thoughts of self-harm or suicide when indicated, following clinical protocol and notifying the appropriate team.

cards.term: Clinical note — scope and plain language
cards.def: Explain within the nurse's role, use plain language, and contact the provider for questions that require medical clarification.

cards.term: Clinical note — do not promise outcomes
cards.def: Do not promise an outcome; refer procedure-specific questions to the appropriate member of the surgical team.
Realistic emotional tone and body language (e.g., 'Speak sharply, glance toward the desk, and interrupt once') that make the scenario believable and indicate the patient's state.
After each skit (about 1 minute), the narrator states the technique demonstrated, what the therapeutic nurse did well, and what the nontherapeutic nurse could do differently.
Clinical note: Explore barriers such as cost, side effects, routines, and food access before discussing options with the care team.
Therapeutic technique used with a grieving family member; ask what support would feel helpful and whether spiritual or cultural practices matter to the family.
Nontherapeutic stock phrases such as 'Everything happens for a reason' that dismiss the person's grief.

cards.term: Do not assume beliefs or rush grief
cards.def: Clinical note: Do not assume the person's beliefs or try to make grief feel better immediately.
Therapeutic technique for a newly confused patient: introduce yourself, calmly state where the patient is and why, and offer a simple next step.
Nontherapeutic response telling the confused patient they are being silly or have nothing to worry about.
Clinical note: New confusion after a procedure requires assessment and prompt reporting; do not assume it is a normal part of aging. Protect the patient from falls.
Therapeutic technique of reflecting the central feeling or meaning back to the patient and allowing them to respond; used with an isolated adolescent.
Nontherapeutic behavior: sighing, checking a phone, looking at the clock, or appearing uninterested during conversation.
Clinical note: Maintain privacy and speak respectfully with adolescents; do not dismiss concerns as 'teen drama.'
Therapeutic technique to clarify what the patient means by 'not worth it' and what matters most to them; used when a patient is considering refusing treatment.
Nontherapeutic response in which the nurse scolds, shames, or implies the patient is giving up by refusing treatment.
Clinical note: Do not pressure the patient; communicate concerns and questions to the oncology team when a patient considers refusing treatment.
Therapeutic technique that recognizes the difficulty of a transition and validates the feeling without judging the person's ability; used with an overwhelmed new parent.
Nontherapeutic response of immediately telling the person what they should do without first listening.

cards.term: Respond to safety concerns and escalate
cards.def: Clinical note: If a parent describes feeling unsafe, unable to care for themselves or the baby, or having thoughts of harm, respond seriously and follow the appropriate assessment and escalation process.
Therapeutic technique: ask a neutral question about pain—its location, severity, timing, or effect on movement.
Nontherapeutic question that suggests the expected answer, such as 'It's not that bad, is it?'

cards.term: Assess pain; do not assume expected complication
cards.def: Clinical note: Assess pain and associated symptoms, follow the care plan, and report concerning changes. Do not assume pain is an expected complication.
Therapeutic technique that acknowledges the hurt and embarrassment without judging appearance; used with a teenager with body image concerns.
Nontherapeutic rapid questioning of personal topics that feels prying before establishing trust.

cards.term: Eating changes and body dissatisfaction warrant follow-up
cards.def: Clinical note: Eating changes and intense body dissatisfaction warrant sensitive follow-up and appropriate assessment; do not reinforce weight stigma or offer appearance-based reassurance.
Therapeutic technique: ask before offering a hand or other appropriate touch, respect the patient's response, and stay present; used with a seriously ill patient afraid of dying.
Nontherapeutic response in which the nurse shifts attention away from the patient by sharing a story about their own experience.
Clinical note: Respect consent, culture, trauma history, and the patient's cues regarding touch; presence and listening are alternatives.
Therapeutic technique: describe the specific behavior (e.g., grimacing, guarding an incision) without accusing the patient of dishonesty, then invite them to explain.
Nontherapeutic behavior of accepting a pain number without further assessment or ignoring behavior that contradicts the self-report.

cards.term: Do not infer pain solely from appearance
cards.def: Clinical note: Do not infer pain solely from appearance or stereotype how a person should express it. Respect self-report and assess further using an open, culturally responsive approach.
Therapeutic technique: ask what name and pronouns the patient uses, use them consistently, and acknowledge the concern; used with a transgender patient.
Nontherapeutic response that dismisses the patient's identity request, argues, or treats identity as irrelevant to respectful care.
Clinical note: Protect privacy and follow applicable documentation and care policies. Do not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team.
Each scenario pairs one therapeutic technique to demonstrate with one nontherapeutic technique to avoid, illustrating the contrast in nurse responses.

Scenarios cover a patient struggling with chronic illness adherence, grieving families, confused elderly patients, isolated adolescents, treatment refusal, new parents, postoperative pain (including a mismatch between the pain rating and the patient's behavior), body image concerns, dying patients, transgender patients, and parents of chronically ill children—each requiring adapted communication.

cards.term: Parent of a chronically ill child
cards.def: Scenario 17 (clinic visit after another hospitalization): a parent expresses distress—"It's not fair that my child has to go through all this." The provided source excerpt ends mid-statement, so the therapeutic and nontherapeutic techniques for this scenario are not specified and should not be assumed from the source.
Allow a brief, attentive silence without rushing to fill it; then follow the parent's lead.
Silence should communicate presence, not withdrawal. Stay attentive and offer support when the parent is ready.
After the pause, the nurse follows the parent's lead rather than steering the conversation away from the emotion.
Relying only on a yes-or-no question cuts off the emotion with a closed question that limits expression.
Work together to identify the immediate concern and realistic next steps, rather than taking over or blaming.
Nontherapeutic problem-solving takes over for the student or assigns blame instead of identifying realistic next steps together.
Discussing the student's situation with others unnecessarily or spreading assumptions is a nontherapeutic response.
Respect confidentiality and clarify when information must be shared for safety or academic support.
Offer time to practice, review the steps together, and identify what the parent wants to work on first.
The nontherapeutic nurse appears rushed, distracted, dismissive, or unprepared.
Use teach-back and supervised return demonstration as appropriate to confirm understanding of instructions.
Use supervised return demonstration as appropriate; the parent practices the skill with the nurse observing.
Never imply that the parent should administer medication without adequate instruction and demonstrated understanding.
Discharge teaching after a child's new diabetes diagnosis addresses the parent's fear of making a mistake with insulin and the volume of steps to remember.
Arrange a qualified medical interpreter for the patient with limited English proficiency when explaining medication and discharge instructions.
Speak directly to the patient in short segments, and pause for interpretation.
The patient speaks limited English, nods politely, but cannot explain when or how to take the medication.
The nontherapeutic nurse raises their voice, relies on gestures alone for complex information, or treats nodding as proof of understanding.
Treating polite nodding as proof of understanding is nontherapeutic; the patient must be able to explain when and how to take the medication.
Do not rely on a child or unqualified bystander to interpret important clinical information when qualified interpretation is available.
Follow organizational policy for interpretation and for applicable documentation and care policies.
Follow applicable documentation and care policies. Do not make the patient responsible for educating the entire team.
After each skit: (1) What did the therapeutic nurse do or say? (2) How did the patient respond? (3) What made the nontherapeutic response ineffective? (4) What could the nurse try next?
Respect the patient's dignity and choices in all communication.
Use plain language and listen before advising.
Notice verbal and nonverbal cues without making assumptions.
Escalate clinical or safety concerns appropriately.

A communication practice exercise in which a scenario, patient acting cues, therapeutic technique, and nontherapeutic counterpart are demonstrated and compared; it is not a substitute for formal support.
A disease state that results from the presence of pathogens in or on the body. A six-part process must occur in order for an infection to occur.
The six-part process of infection: infectious agent, reservoir, portal of exit, means of transmission, portal of entry, susceptible host. Nursing interventions target breaking this chain.

Microorganisms that cause disease: bacteria (E. coli, staphylococcus, streptococcus), viruses (HIV, common cold, influenza, COVID-19, hepatitis A,B,C), fungi (athlete's foot, ringworm, yeast infections), parasites (malaria from mosquitos infected with a parasite).
Potential sources where pathogens live: people, animals, soil, food, water, milk, objects.
Routes pathogens enter the human body: respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary tracts, skin breakdown, blood & tissues.
Routes pathogens leave the human body: respiratory, gastrointestinal, genitourinary tracts, skin breakdown, blood & drainage.
Direct contact: close proximity, touching, kissing, sexual intercourse. Indirect contact occurs through a vector or a fomite.
A living creature that transmits a pathogen to humans.
An inanimate object that harbors a pathogen. Nurses' equipment and objects in the environment can act as fomites.
Organisms greater than 5um (micrometer) attach to dust particles. Droplets are heavy enough to land on surfaces.
Organisms less than 5um (micrometer) attach to dust particles. Airborne particles remain in the air.

A host at risk for infection: multiple wounds/poor skin integrity (multiple portals of entry), pH levels of GI and GU tracts and skin, WBC count, age, sex, heredity, immunity, fatigue, nutritional status, pre-existing illness, medications, stress, and invasive or indwelling medical devices.
Immunity may be natural, acquired, or passive. It is one factor determining whether a host is susceptible.

cards.term: Factors that make an organism thrive
cards.def: Quantity of organism, virulence, the patient's immune system, how long the organism + patient were in contact, and what type of contact they had.
Four stages: incubation period, prodromal stage, full stage of illness, and convalescent period.
The stage before symptoms appear; examples: common cold 1-2 days, tetanus 2-21 days.
Lasts hours to days; the patient may report nonspecific symptoms such as being too tired to hold up the head with a low-grade fever.
The stage in which the infectious illness is fully manifested, following the prodromal stage and preceding convalescence.
Illness resolved, period of recovery, return to baseline health. There may be a temporary or permanent change in the patient's previous health.
A person can continuously cycle through the same infectious process; HSV is the example given.
Methods to prevent infection, divided into medical asepsis ("clean technique") and surgical asepsis ("sterile technique").

Reduces the number of pathogens: hand hygiene, wearing gloves, not placing dirty/soiled linen on the floor, avoiding raising dust, practicing clean-to-dirty technique, disposing of dirty linens directly into the hamper, and pouring contaminated liquids directly into the drain or "hopper" to prevent splashing.

Eliminates the number of pathogens by creating and maintaining a pathogen-free environment. Required for procedures such as foley catheters and central line placement/dressing changes; uses sterile gloves, mask, hair net, gowns, etc.
Practice moving from clean to dirty areas/objects when providing care to reduce the number of pathogens transferred.
1) Before touching a patient, 2) before a clean or aseptic procedure, 3) after body fluid exposure risk, 4) after touching a patient, 5) after touching patient surroundings.
Also known as hospital acquired/nosocomial infections; infections patients develop during hospitalization.
Catheter Associated Urinary Tract Infections (CAUTI), Surgical Site Infection (SSI), Central-Line Associated Bloodstream Infection (CLABSI), and Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia (VAP).
Vancomycin Resistant Enterococci; a multidrug-resistant organism found in feces, urine, and blood.
Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus; found in the nares, on the skin, or in the GI tract.
Carbapenem-Resistant Enterobacteriaceae; a multidrug-resistant organism prevalent in hospitalized patients.
Clostridium Difficile; a multidrug-resistant organism found in feces.
Equipment used to protect the nurse: gloves, gown, masks, and protective eye-wear.

Used in the care of all hospitalized patients regardless of their diagnosis or possible infection status. Apply to blood, all body fluids, secretions, and excretions except sweat (whether blood is present or visible), non-intact skin, and mucous membranes.
Respiratory hygiene/cough etiquette, safe injection practices, and directions to use a mask when performing high-risk prolonged procedures involving spinal canal punctures.
Used in addition to standard precautions for patients with suspected infection with pathogens transmitted by airborne, droplet, or contact routes. A disease may have multiple routes of transmission.
Proper donning of PPE when entering the room of a patient on contact or droplet precautions; proper doffing of PPE when leaving the room.
Infection spreads by large particle droplets. Private room, door can stay open, surgical mask and gloves.
For patients infected or colonized by a multi drug resistant organism (MDRO). Private room, gown and gloves, change gloves after contacting infective material, clean all equipment; do not share.
For infections that spread through the air. Private room, negative air pressure, door closed, patient remains in room, respirator mask; surgical mask on patient for transport.
Recommended for severely immunocompromised & immunosuppressed residents receiving any cancer treatment or transplants. Applies to residents with WBC below 500 cells/mm3 (µL).
