cards.def: Indicators of physiologic functioning that reflect the health status of a person. Include temperature, pulse, respirations, blood pressure, pulse oximetry, and pain level.

On admission, per facility policy, any change in patient's condition, loss of consciousness, before/after surgical or invasive procedures, before/after high-risk activity (e.g., ambulation after surgery), before administering cardiovascular/respiratory medications, or whenever the patient reports change in status, pain, or distress.

The hypothalamus controls thermoregulation by conserving body heat or increasing heat loss. It reflects the difference between the amount of heat produced by the body and the amount of heat lost to the environment.
Core body temp locations include intracranial, intrathoracic, and intra-abdominal sites. These are the most accurate sources for core temperature.
The body's tissues and cells function best between 36°C to 37.5°C (98.6°F).
Predictable fluctuations in body temperature—lower in the morning, peak between 1500-1800.

Time of day, biologic sex, age, physical activity, state of health, and environmental temperatures. Older adults' sensitivity to temperature changes is decreased; extreme cold may lead to hypothermia, extreme heat may lead to hyperthermia.
When a patient has an increased temperature they are considered febrile; non-fever is afebrile. Signs/symptoms include loss of appetite, headache, hot dry skin, thirst, muscle aches and fatigue.
Extremely high temperature above 40°C (>104°F) is dangerous; ≥41°C (106°F) is a medical emergency.

Fever is a sign of immune response and an important defense mechanism. Treatment aims to provide comfort and prevent complications: pharmaceutical (antipyretics; treatment of bacterial infection) and non-pharmaceutical (cool bath, cooling blankets, removing excess clothing/blankets, oral fluids to prevent dehydration).

Symptoms include poor coordination, slurred speech, amnesia, hallucinations, stupor; respirations, HR, and B/P decrease. Treatment: raise body temp and promote warmth with warm blankets, warm fluids, and Bair Hugger.

Place thermometer in posterior sublingual pocket under the tongue (close to carotid artery). No hot/cold drinks or smoking 20 min prior; patient must be awake and alert. Not for small children. Leave in place 3 min.

Place bulb in center of axilla with lower arm positioned across chest. Non-invasive and good for children but less accurate (no major vessels nearby). Leave in place 5-10 min. Measures 0.5°C lower than oral temp.

Side lying with upper leg flexed; insert lubricated bulb 1-1½ inch for adults. Used when unsafe or inaccurate by mouth (unconscious, disoriented, or irrational). Leave in place 2-3 min. Measures 0.5°C higher than oral.
Close to hypothalamus and sensitive to core temp changes. For adults, pull pinna up and back. Rapid measurement (2-3 seconds) but cerumen impaction or otitis media can distort reading.

Left ventricle contracts causing a wave of blood to surge through arteries; felt by palpating artery lightly against underlying bone or muscle. Assess rate, rhythm, and amplitude via palpation and auscultation.
Carotid, brachial, radial, femoral, popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis.

Place 2nd, 3rd, or 4th fingers lightly on skin where an artery passes over an underlying bone. Do not use your thumb. Count 30 seconds × 2; if irregular, count radial for 1 min and then apically for a full minute.
The beat of the heart at its apex or point of maximal impulse. Auscultate for a full minute, listening for "Lub-Dub." Auscultate for apical; palpate for peripheral pulses.
Normal adult pulse rate is 60-100 bpm with an average of 80 bpm.
An abnormal increase in pulse rate (above 100 bpm).
An abnormal decrease in pulse rate (below 60 bpm).
The pattern of the beats—assessed as regular or irregular.

The volume of blood pushed against the wall of an artery during ventricular contraction. Described as weak/thready (lacks fullness), full/bounding (volume higher than normal), or imperceptible (cannot be felt or heard).
Gas exchange between oxygen and carbon dioxide; both autonomic and voluntary. Inspiration is inhalation (breathing in) and expiration is exhalation (breathing out).
Observe rate, rhythm, and depth after taking pulse while still holding the hand, so the patient is unaware you are counting respirations.
Normal adult respiratory rate is 12-20 breaths/min; 1 cycle = inhale + exhale.
Abnormal increase in respiratory rate (above 20 breaths/min).
Abnormal decrease in respiratory rate (below 12 breaths/min).
Absence of breathing (periods of no breathing).
Difficulty or labored breathing; adventitious digressions from normal effortless breathing. Orthopnea is difficulty breathing laying down.
Force exerted by the blood against vessel walls. Systolic is the highest pressure created during contraction; diastolic is the lowest pressure on artery walls during relaxation.
Normal is less than 120/80 mmHg.
Readings lower than 90 mmHg systolic or 60 mmHg diastolic.
Systolic between 120-129 and diastolic of 80 mmHg. ⚠ Cheat sheet: diastolic less than 80.
Systolic 130-139 mmHg, diastolic 80-89 mmHg.
Systolic >140 mmHg, diastolic >90 mmHg.
Blood pressure greater than 180 mmHg systolic. This is a critical emergency situation.

Cuff size is judged by arm circumference, not age. Cuff should cover 40% of arm circumference and bladder should cover 2/3 of the arm. Support arm at heart level, palm upward; above heart causes false low reading. Cuff too wide = false low; too narrow or too loose = false high.
A series of sounds created as blood flows through an artery after it has been occluded with a cuff and cuff pressure is gradually released.
Do not use a limb with a PICC line, arteriovenous (AV) fistula, or on the side of a mastectomy for blood pressure assessment.
Non-invasive measurement of oxygen saturation; calculates SpO2 (pulse oxygen saturation) as a reliable estimate of arterial oxygen saturation. Probes can be placed on finger, ear, nose, or toe.
Remove thick nail polish. Wait until readout reaches constant value and pulse display reaches full strength. During continuous monitoring, inspect skin under the probe routinely and rotate the probe.
A pain assessment tool used for verbal, aware patients to evaluate pain.
Assessment data that may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition in addition to changes that occur progressively over time.
A baseline set of VS are important to identify changes in the patient's condition.
VS may reveal sudden changes in a client's condition; a deviation from baseline signals a status change.
Changes in a client's condition that occur progressively over time and are detected through VS measurement.
A change identified by comparing current VS to the client's baseline; the learner is asked, 'What do you think is the source of his change in health status?'
An assessment finding judged to be within the expected or standard range of values.
The benchmark values used for comparison when judging VS findings.
A client's normal range can be different from our standard values; individual norms must be considered.
Considerations that go 'besides numbers' when assessing VS.
When assessing VS, consider factors other than the numeric values alone.
The data used as the basis to identify and prioritize client problems related to vital signs.
Based upon assessment information, identify and prioritize the top 3 client problems related to vital signs.
Ranking the identified vital sign–related problems, e.g., the top 3 client problems, to guide care.
The highest-priority problems related to vital signs selected from the assessment findings.
A vital sign that may be elevated and require interventions to decrease it prior to medication administration.
Interventions taken to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration.
Actions the nurse can take to assist with decreasing the temperature prior to medication administration.
Temperature-lowering interventions are implemented prior to medication administration.
A vital sign that may be increased in the patient; an increased respiratory rate prompts further assessment.
Since the patient has an increased respiratory rate, additional assessment is conducted to determine if he has adequate oxygenation.
Determined by conducting further assessment when the patient has an increased respiratory rate.
Additional assessment conducted to determine if the client with an increased respiratory rate has adequate oxygenation.
A baseline set of VS plus current values are important to identify changes in the patient's condition.
A client's normal range can be different from our standard values, so values are judged in context of the individual client.

Below 90 systolic or below 60 diastolic
120–129 systolic and less than 80 diastolic
Over 180 / over 120 (emergency)
Below 95°F (35°C)
Over 104°F (40°C)
Over 106°F (41°C), medical emergency
Less than 60 bpm
More than 100 bpm
12–20 breaths/min
Less than 12 breaths/min
More than 20 breaths/min
Below 92%
Dark longer lines = 10s; light shorter lines = 2s; report even numbers only
